Disciplinary proceedings initiated against 3 cops over alleged involvement in Karachi DHA residents' scuffle: DIG. KARACHI: Disciplinary proceedings were initiated on Sunday against three cops for their alleged involvement in a recent scuffle between two apartment residents in Defence Housing Authority’s (DHA) Phase 6, a police officer said. The development comes after the CCTV footage of the incident , which took place on August 21, went viral on social media. South Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Syed Asad Raza told Dawn that formal proceedings have been initiated in the matter and the policemen allegedly involved in the incident have been identified. The three were directed to appear before the South DIG tomorrow (Monday) at his office for disciplinary proceedings. DIG Raza also told Dawn that both parties have been asked to attend the inquiry proceedings. Additionally, neighbours were also asked to provide information about the incident and relevant digital evidence. Earlier in the day, Karachi Additional Inspector General (AIG) Azad Khan had sought a report within three days on the scuffle and the alleged involvement and “misconduct” of police personnel in the matter. AIG Khan ordered a “complete and unbiased” inquiry into the incident, instructing the South deputy inspector general to submit a report within three days, an official police statement said. He sought a “fact-based report” on the alleged misconduct of police personnel in the matter, it added. The AIG directed that all aspects of the case should be assessed and those involved should be identified, according to the statement. On Saturday, DIG Raza had told Dawn that he had directed the investigation officer to conduct a probe on merit and in an impartial manner. CCTV and FIR In the CCTV footage of the incident, a woman can be seen rushing down a flight of stairs with a dumbbell in her hand and charging at another woman before using it to hit her. The video also showed two individuals in what appeared to be police uniforms restraining the woman being assaulted, and a man who came up the stairs shortly after and began arguing with the woman with the dumbbell. At one point, the man and woman being assaulted managed to go inside what appeared to be their home, following which the woman with a dumbbell and another man began banging on their door and yelling obscenities. At the end, a man in a shalwar kameez can be seen using a weapon, provided by one of the people in uniform, to smash the CCTV camera. But the incident’s first information report (FIR) offered a different version of events. It was registered at Darakhshan police station at 1:40am on Aug 21 on the complaint of a woman. The FIR seen by Dawn invoked Sections 354 (assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty), 504 (intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of the peace), 506 (criminal intimidation), 337A(i) (punishment of shajjah ), 382 (theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint to commit theft) and 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code. However, DIG Raza said that Section 382 pertaining to the alleged theft of gold ornaments had been removed from the FIR as the incident appeared to be a case of assault. In the complaint, the woman described herself as a resident of the fourth floor of an apartment building, adding that a man, his sister and their mother — who resided on the third floor — came to their door and started kicking it. The complainant alleged that the three family members hurled verbal abuses over a parking issue, and upon opening the door, began beating and threatening her. Subsequently, local police arrived on the spot and took the brother and sister into custody on the complainant’s statement, while their mother fled, the FIR said. In the FIR, the woman also claimed that the other side “snatched” her gold earring and two rings.

Nepal-China flood death toll rises to nearly 800, with over 3,000 missing. Devastating floods near the border with China killed at least 781 people in Nepal, its disaster authority said on Sunday, with 2,502 people missing as rescue efforts continued for a fifth day. Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 dead in Tibet and 546 people missing following Wednesday’s disaster , taking the overall toll to 797 dead and 3,048 unaccounted for. Nepal’s missing list includes 592 foreigners unaccounted for. It also includes 933 workers on hydropower projects along the river which the torrent crashed through, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Nepal’s disaster agency listed 1,910 missing citizens in an update on Sunday. That includes 562 unaccounted for in the hardest-hit district of Rasuwa. In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims. However, they are not included in the toll. The Red Cross has estimated that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster, which China has linked to the effects of climate change. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his Nepalese counterpart during a Saturday telephone call that the mudslide was their “most severe cross-border disaster” in recent years and that rescue operations had risen to an unprecedented level of difficulty and complexity, state broadcaster CCTV reported. On the Chinese side, authorities said 16 people were killed in Gyirong County, and 546 were missing. Beijing said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were unaccounted for in Tibet, near a key border crossing with Nepal. The scale of the disaster has complicated rescue efforts across the rugged Himalayan terrain. Local police in Nepal told Reuters that residents and rescue workers had moved to higher ground after the Trishuli River’s water levels rose in recent hours following fresh rainfall, raising fears of additional flooding. Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s Lhende Khola and Trishuli Rivers. CCTV reported that the lake threatening downstream areas had been largely drained by Saturday evening. But drones detected a landslide late on Saturday that is 2.8 kilometres downstream of the lake, forming a new dam and a fresh pool of water. In Nepal, rescue efforts have become more focused on hundreds of people believed to be trapped inside tunnels at hydropower plants damaged by the floods. Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said Nepal required international assistance in specialised areas, including tunnel rescue operations, DNA testing, refrigerated storage for bodies and forensic identification of decomposed remains. Indian and Chinese experts were already working to help open tunnels and support rescue operations, Chhetri said. Mass burials of decomposing bodies Days after desperate relatives moved between hospitals, morgues and relief centres searching for loved ones, authorities in Nepal began mass burials of hundreds of unidentified victims whose bodies had started to decompose. In Chitwan district, which escaped the direct impact of the disaster, bodies swept downstream from the flood-hit Rasuwa region have been carried by the river system into the Narayani River. Authorities are photographing the bodies, collecting DNA samples and recording identifying details in the hope that families may still be able to identify relatives after burial. “Of the bodies we have recovered so far, more than half are beyond recognition,” police officer Anil Thapa told Reuters. “Many have no visible faces. In some cases, only hands or legs remain; in others, only parts of the body are available. In many cases, more than half of the head is missing.” After burying more than 100 unidentified bodies on Saturday, authorities were digging additional graves on Sunday for hundreds more. Link to ‘long-term effects of climate change’ The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, CCTV reported, saying it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters” on the Tibetan plateau. The mudslide from the Nepalese side took six to seven minutes to reach the Gyirong border crossing, CCTV said, citing the findings of Chinese scientists. Dramatic surveillance footage shared worldwide showed torrents of water and debris engulfing buildings while people tried to flee. The state-run TV channel reported China has mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least 220 million yuan ($32.7m) to support relief efforts and has been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing.

'They can come to Pakistan today': Khawaja Asif disputes claim by Imran's sons of expired Nicops. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif on Sunday said that PTI founder Imran Khan’s sons — Qasim and Sulaiman Khan — could visit Pakistan “today if they wished”, citing the validity of their National Identity Cards for Overseas Pakistanis (Nicop). The government has consistently maintained that Imran’s children can enter the country based on their Nicops with no visa required. However, the sons claimed earlier this month that their Nicops have expired and accused the government of denying them visas. In a post on social media platform X, the defence minister recalled that the ex-premier’s sons had last travelled to Pakistan on their Nicops in November 2022 , when the PTI founder got injured in an assassination attempt . “They can visit Pakistan today if they wish. Both Nicops are valid,” Asif stated. He also shared partially censored Nicop numbers for both Kasim and Sulaiman, stating that the document was valid until Nov 8, 2032 for Kasim and Jan 6, 2030, for Suleman. The minister dismissed the perception that the government was denying them visas as “incorrect”, accusing Imran’s family and PTI of concocting the narrative. “Holders of Nicops can travel to Pakistan whenever they wish. There is no need for a visa,” he maintained. A day earlier, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (MOIB) had addressed the potential arrival of Imran’s sons, noting that they may enter the country through their Nicops, but that access to the country may not guarantee access to prison visitation. Zulfi Bukhari, adviser to Imran on foreign media, responded to the government’s stance on his recent CNN interview with a lengthy statement. He reiterated his claims of the PTI founder being kept in “solitary confinement” and detailed medical concerns raised in a doctor’s assessment submitted to the Supreme Court. Sons want to meet their father As Kasim and his older brother Suleiman live in London with their mother and Imran’s former spouse Jemima Goldsmith, they will have to travel to Pakistan to meet Imran, who is imprisoned at Rawalpindi’s Adiala jail. In December 2025, Kasim had said that he and his brother had applied for their visas. However, in February, Kasim claimed that the government was “deliberately” refusing to process his and his brother’s visas. The next month, Goldsmith made a “direct appeal” to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to grant her sons visas. In response to the appeal, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said that Imran’s children were welcome to visit Pakistan on their Nicops. Meanwhile, Goldsmith alleged that the government was recommending that her sons travel to Pakistan on Nicops as they would have “no British protection”, expressing fear that they may be arrested on arrival. In her statement, Goldsmith had claimed that the government was refusing her sons’ visas and held that they also did not have their renewed Nicops. Imran was sent to jail on August 5, 2023, in the Toshakhana case. However, he is also serving a 14-year sentence in a £190 million corruption case , was convicted in another Toshakhana case in December 2025 and also faces pending trials in terrorism cases related to the May 9, 2023 riots . The ex-premier’s sons, along with his party and family, have been protesting against the lack of meetings and phone calls with him despite court orders for the same.

England clinch series win over Pakistan with thumping 194-run victory in second Test. Ollie Robinson led the way once more as England clinched a series win over Pakistan with a thumping 194-run win in the second Test at Lord’s on Sunday despite Saud Shakeel’s fine 97. Pakistan were dismissed for 194, having been set an improbable victory target of 389, to give England an unbeatable 2-0 lead in a three-match series. This was England’s first multi-match Test series win since a 2-1 success in New Zealand more than a year ago. Robinson finished with figures of 4-24 in 14 overs following his sensational 4-11 in 13 during Pakistan’s meagre first-innings 110 all out. The Sussex seamer produced a pair of double strikes Sunday either side of Shakeel and Shan Masood, checking England’s progress with a fourth-wicket partnership of 97. Robinson took two wickets in four balls to leave the tourists 7-2, before express quick Jofra Archer dismissed Pakistan captain Babar Azam. But from the dire position of 14-3 before lunch, Shakeel and fellow left-hander Masood kept England at bay. Robinson, however, had Masood lbw from around the wicket for a gritty 26 off 72 balls, although it needed a review to reverse umpire Allahuddien Paleker’s original not out decision. And 111-4 became 115-5 when Mohammad Rizwan was lbw to Robinson carelessly slogging across the line. Shakeel, 78 not out at tea, went to 86 by hooking Tongue for six and, two balls later, another superb hook off another the fast bowler saw him into the 90s. Shakeel pulled the fifth ball of the over to go to 96 only to hole out soon afterwards when he swung Tongue straight to Harry Brook at deep square leg. A crestfallen Shakeel received a standing ovation from MCC members in the pavilion as he walked back in after the end of a 122-ball innings also featuring 13 fours. Pakistan were now 169-7, although they were effectively eight wickets down with Imam-ul-Haq still sidelined by the calf problem, meaning he was unable to bat in Pakistan’s first innings. Tongue then cemented his reputation for polishing off the tail by bowling Khurram Shahzad before ending the match when he had Mohammad Ali caught in the slips by Brook. Pakistan had looked to Masood and Azan Awais to see off the new ball on a still seam-friendly pitch. Awais, however, was lbw to Robinson and, three balls later, Abdullah Shafique was bowled for a duck by a superb delivery from the paceman that angled in and moved away late to hit off stump. Archer’s brute of a bouncer then had Azam in a horrible flap, with the ball looping to Jordan Cox at second slip. Abbas on the honours board at last Earlier, Mohammad Abbas finally achieved a coveted place on the Lord’s honours boards with a return of 5-57 as England were dismissed for 208. Cricketers who take at least five wickets in an innings or 10 in a match or score a century in a Test at Lord’s have their feats recorded on one of the honours boards in the home and away dressing rooms at the ‘Home of Cricket’. Abbas, 36, had come close before with a trio of four-wicket hauls, including his 4-73 in England’s first-innings 290 of this match. But he went one better Sunday after starting the day with 3-48. Dan Lawrence had added just four runs to his overnight 50 not out when he was bowled by Abbas before the veteran seamer had Robinson edging to wicket-keeper Rizwan, who held a fine catch standing up to the stumps. An elated Abbas was mobbed by his teammates before kissing the turf in celebration.

Bannu police peace committee submits 11-point assurance as talks conclude. BANNU: Successful talks between the Police Peace Committee and police officials concluded on Sunday, with the former submitting an 11-point written assurance, which outlines a code of conduct for committee members. Under the assurance, submitted to the regional police officer (RPO) and district police officer (DPO), peace committee members will not participate in protests, strikes, sit-ins or political activities and will perform their duties within the framework of the law. According to the written assurance, no committee member will arrest any person without legal authority. Action against individuals wanted in terrorism or other serious cases will be taken through the relevant law enforcement agencies, particularly the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD). Committee members will cooperate with the army, Frontier Corps (FC), CTD and other law enforcement agencies (LEAs) only on the directions of authorised officials. The assurance also stated that members will refrain from exceeding their authority and engaging in unlawful activities, while accepting legal action in case of any violation of the code. The talks were held at Bannu Police Lines and were attended by RPO Bannu Abdul Ghafoor Afridi, MNA Maulana Syed Naseem Ali Shah, MNA Sher Afzal Khan Marwat, MPA Malik Pakhtunyar Khan and other local elders. During the talks, estranged PTI leader Marwat expressed reservations over the transfers of Police Peace Committee members, saying that instead of transferring them, authorities should examine why the committee was formed in the first place and what circumstances compelled police personnel to take such a step. Earlier this week, Police Peace Committee President Hazratullah objected to the transfer of seven Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police constables to other districts. He called on the personnel to boycott their duties, resulting in disruptions to police services and the traffic system in several areas. The MNA affirmed that the 2.2 million people of Bannu and Lakki Marwat stood with the Police Peace Committee. He said sacrifices in the region had created hope among the people and that the situation was gradually improving. He urged authorities to avoid steps that could undermine the committee’s role, warning that if weakening the committee resulted in terrorists becoming active again, the responsibility would rest with the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa inspector general. He urged Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, KP IG Zulfiqar Hameed and the chief secretary to resolve issues concerning the Police Peace Committee through consultation at the local level and to take all stakeholders into confidence on matters relating to peace and security. Meanwhile, MNA Shah called for the formation of district-level empowered committees for future decisions concerning the police in Bannu and Lakki Marwat, saying that decisions should not be imposed without local consultation. MPA Pakhtunyar stated that he stood with the police and the Police Peace Committee, adding that if any attempt was made to create obstacles in their way or undermine their role, he would stand firmly with both the police and the committee. Meanwhile, in Lakki Marwat, the Police Peace Committee ended its four-day protest following talks with the Bannu RPO in the presence of Marwat. During the negotiations, assurances were given for the recovery of an abducted police official, who was subsequently recovered. The talks also covered the cancellation of transfers of certain police personnel and local elders, provision of modern equipment to the police and improvement of security arrangements. It has also been decided to seek FC’s services for the security of sensitive locations in Bannu and Lakki Marwat. Bannu district has been the scene of repeated security incidents in recent months, with both civilians and local security forces coming under attack amid a broader surge in militant violence. On August 10, a police constable was martyred when unidentified armed men opened fire on him in the district’s Sorani area. The same day, the district police, CTD and security forces conducted a joint operation in the jurisdiction of the Miryan police station, leading to the killing of an unidentified terrorist and the arrest of 10 suspected individuals. Days later, the police and security forces claimed to have killed five terrorists and injured several others during a joint intelligence-based operation in parts of Domel tehsil. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies , an Islamabad-based think tank, violence linked to terrorist attacks and counter-terrorism operations intensified sharply in July, making it the deadliest month of 2026, with 112 security personnel among 205 people killed.

Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye to hold first meeting under Makkah pact in Istanbul on Monday. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye will hold their first meeting under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Istanbul on Monday, the Foreign Office (FO) confirmed. In a statement, FO said the “inaugural meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee established under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (Makkah Accord)” will be held in the Turkish capital. Pakistan will be represented at the meeting by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, and Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir. The meeting will also be attended by the respective foreign and defence ministers, as well as the chiefs of general staff, of Turkiye and Saudi Arabia, according to FO. “Pakistan’s participation in the meeting signifies Pakistan’s historic bonds of friendship with the brotherly countries of Turkiye and Saudi Arabia, as well as its desire for lasting regional peace and stability,” the statement highlighted. Chief of the Army Staff Munir arrived “in Turkiye on an official visit”, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said in a brief statement issued in the evening. In its statement, Turkiye said FM Hakan Fidan, Defence Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of Turkish General Staff Gen Selcuk Bayraktaroglu will participate in the meeting. ‘Continued strengthening’ of Pak-Turkiye ties Earlier in the day, FM Dar reached Istanbul after concluding his visit to the United Kingdom. He then held a meeting with FM Fidan, with both sides expressing “satisfaction at the continued strengthening and expansion of bilateral relations in the political, economic, security and cultural domains”, FO said on X. The foreign ministers welcomed the progress achieved under the framework of the Pakistan–Türkiye High-Level Strategic Cooperation Council (HLSCC) and agreed on the early convening of its next session. “The two sides also exchanged views on issues of regional and international importance and reaffirmed their commitment to continue working closely for regional peace and stability,” the statement read. Special Secretary (United Nations) Nabeel Munir, Director General (UN) Umar Siddique, First Secretary Qazi Saleem, and Deputy Director to the Foreign Minister Agha Hunain also joined Dar for the meeting. Upon his arrival in Istanbul, Dar was received by Turkish Deputy Chief of Staff for Administration Brig. General Senol Varol, Pakistan’s Ambassador to Turkiye Dr Yousaf Junaid, Ambassador Cihad Erginay of the Turkish foreign ministry, and other senior officials of the Turkish government, FO said. The deputy premier later visited the shrine of Hazrat Abu Ayyub Ansari (RA) to pay his respects. He offered prayers for the peace and prosperity of Pakistan and its people, as well as for the Muslim community’s unity, FO said. Earlier this month, Turkiye’s Fidan had also invited Dar to the Regional-4 meeting in Istanbul, which includes the three countries part of the defence pact, along with Egypt. Dar had confirmed his participation in the meeting, which was scheduled to take place in August, FO had said. The R-4 group has been focused on regional security and emerged in March amid efforts for mediation between the US and Iran. The last R-4 meeting was held on August 5 in Amman , where the ministers “reaffirmed the importance of continued consultation and close coordination among the four countries in advancing regional stability”, according to FO. Prior to that, a Cairo meeting held in June welcomed the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding between the US and Iran. The first and second R-4 meetings — both held in March — took place in Riyadh and Islamabad , respectively. UK visit wrapped up In an earlier statement, FO said DPM Dar “concluded a successful official visit to the UK”. During his trip, Dar met several officials, including UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, Minister of State for Pakistan Stephen Doughty, National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, International Maritime Organisation (IMO) Secretary General Arsenio Dominguez and Commonwealth Secretary General Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey. The deputy premier also interacted with British parliamentarians of Pakistani origin and the Pakistani diaspora in the UK.

Armed clash between two clans claims 8 lives in Sindh's Dadu. HYDERABAD: Eight individuals were killed while two others were injured in an armed clash between two groups of the Chandio clan in Dadu district in the early hours of Sunday. According to a police report, the feud between the two sides was the result of an “ongoing blood feud and disputes regarding the use of a common passage and other land-related matters”. The incident took place in the jurisdiction of the Jhallo police station. Hyderabad Range Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Tariq Dharejo confirmed the incident, adding that the deceased were wanted in some criminal cases by police as well. Out of eight deceased, two belonged to Sikandar Chandio’s group, and six belonged to Ali Akber Chandio’s side. He said that efforts had been underway to bring about reconciliation between the two sides, but in vain. The deceased from Sikandar Chandio’s group were identified as Usman Chandio’s son Deedar Ali and his brother, Gul Bahar. Usman’s son Mumtaz and Kehar Khan Chandio’s son Ghulam Qadir were injured from the group. Meanwhile, the deceased from Ali Akbar Chandio’s side included Gahi Khan’s son Fida Hussain; Zulfiqar alias Watani, son of Mohammad Waris Chandio; Mohammad Bachal, son of Mohammad Bux Chandio; Akbar Chandio’s sons Sultan and Manzoor; and Arshad alias Hajjan, son of Usman Chandio. The deceased and injured were shifted to the Dadu District Headquarters Hospital. DIG Dharejo said that the two sides had exchanged gunshots on several occasions in the last three years because they were at loggerheads. These clashes had earlier also caused the deaths of two persons each from both sides. Nine others had received injuries, while their cases were pending in court. He noted that among the deceased, Gul Bahar was involved in eight cases, Fida Hussain in one, Zulfiqar in seven, Bachal in 11, Manzoor in five and Arshad alias Hajjan in one case as per police record. Injured Ghulam Qadir was involved in two cases. Dadu Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Mir Saddam told Dawn that the incident took place Sunday morning when Ali Akbar Chandio’s men attacked Sikandar Chandio-Khan Mohammad Chandio side, leading to a fierce clash and ending up in multiple deaths. He added that some arrests have been made by police and weapons were recovered. The bodies from both sides were unburied as of Sunday evening. SSP Saddam disclosed that Ali Akbar Chandio wanted to avenge the killing of his school-going nephew because Ali Akbar’s brother had not agreed to the reconciliation proposal involving Khan Mohammad Chandio. He said that the area where casualties took place was mostly a riverine area. “Police have been deployed there to control the situation from escalating any further,” he said.

Islamabad, Riyadh agree to boost Pakistani agri and food exports to $3bn. Islamabad and Riyadh have agreed to boost Pakistani agricultural and food exports to Saudi Arabia up to $3 billion, the countries said in a joint statement on Sunday. The statement, shared by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), said the agreement was reached after “successful” talks between Saudi Arabia’s agriculture ministry and Pakistan’s food security ministry, at the initiative of PM Shehbaz Sharif. At the invitation of the Pakistani government, a Saudi delegation led by Minister of Environment, Water and Agriculture Engineer Abdulrahman Al-Fadley visited Islamabad from August 26 to August 28. The delegation included senior officials from Riyadh’s Ministry of Environment, Water and Agriculture, the General Food Security Authority and other relevant institutions. PM Shehbaz met the Saudi delegation and discussed potential areas of cooperation in detail, the joint statement said, referring to Friday’s meeting. “The two countries expressed their shared commitment to increase Pakistan’s agricultural and food exports to Saudi Arabia to $3bn, with efforts to be made to achieve the target over the next two years,” it read. “For this purpose, rice, red meat, fruits and their concentrates, green fodder and water-efficient agricultural technologies were identified as priority sectors in collaboration with the Saudi private sector.” During the visit, the two sides held briefings on the Pakistan-Saudi Arabia Agriculture and Food Strategic Plan and meetings with the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC), Fauji Foundation and the Pakistan-Saudi Arabia Agri-Business Forum. The Saudi delegation also visited the National Agricultural Research Centre (NARC). Reaffirming their deep and historic ties, the two sides highlighted the strong alignment between Saudi Arabia’s food security priorities under Vision 2030 and Pakistan’s agricultural and food export sector. The delegations noted that Pakistan supplied around 169,000 tonnes of rice worth about $163 million to the Saudi market in 2025. The Saudi team expressed interest in further increasing bilateral rice trade in the coming years, according to the joint statement. Furthermore, the Saudi delegation expressed interest in gradually doubling imports of red meat from Pakistan, as both sides reviewed Islamabad’s annual supply of around 30,000 tonnes of red meat worth approximately $167m. Regarding fruits and fruit concentrates, the two sides highlighted significant potential to further increase Pakistan’s share of the Saudi market. They encouraged measures to facilitate business-to-business linkages and matchmaking between the private sectors of the two countries, as well as the mutual recognition of quality certifications. The Saudi side identified green fodder as a promising area for expanding trade and establishing long-term supply partnerships, the joint statement said. Both countries welcomed the successful completion of the first phase of a water-efficient irrigation programme in Punjab’s Bhakkar and expressed interest in a proposed second phase targeting small farmers. The Saudi delegation also encouraged Pakistan to join the International Dates Council, a proposal welcomed by the Pakistani side. The two sides also reviewed investment proposals put forward by Pakistan’s private sector in livestock, agri-food processing and the rice value chain, and agreed to maintain coordination to pursue cooperation in these areas. “Both countries reaffirmed their broader strategic partnership,” the statement read. Pakistan also welcomed an invitation to participate in the 43rd Saudi Agriculture Exhibition, scheduled to be held in Riyadh from October 19 to 22. Both sides expressed satisfaction with the outcomes of the visit and agreed to maintain coordination to translate the understandings reached into practical cooperation. The Pakistani delegation was led by Minister for National Food Security and Research Rana Tanveer Hussain and included its Secretary Aamir Ali Ahmed, Commerce Secretary Jawad Paul, PM’s Coordinator for Agriculture and Food Security Ahmed Umair, and private-sector representatives from Pakistan’s rice, red meat, processed food/fruit concentrate and green fodder sectors. Prior to the Saudi delegation’s visit this week, Assistant Minister of Investment of Saudi Arabia Ibrahim Al-Mubarak had toured Islamabad in February, when he expressed interest in investing in corporate farming in Pakistan’s rice sector.

At least 8 die, more missing, as ferry capsizes off Northern Cyprus. A passenger ferry capsized and sank off Northern Cyprus on Sunday, killing at least eight people and leaving more than a dozen missing, officials and media reports said, as police took the captain and seven crew members into custody. Several rescued passengers told local media a blast had gone off at the bow of the ferry before it rolled over, and said the boat had an insufficient supply of life-vests. The vessel capsized 6.5 kilometres off the coast of Cyprus, shortly after leaving a Northern Cyprus port bound for Turkiye’s mainland. Images broadcast by Turkish television showed the upside-down ferry in the water, with people wearing life vests atop its orange hull. “Some people had to jump without lifebuoys or life jackets,” one young man, Efe Multici, told CNN Turk . “It was literally a fight for survival.” The ferry had been carrying a total of 267 people, according to authorities, of which 161 were rescued and taken to hospital and 76 have returned home. The official Cypriot news agency TAK , however, said 17 were missing. The ferry had departed from the Northern Cyprus port of Kyrenia — called Girne Kepuveia in Turkish — heading to the Turkish port of Tasucu. Captain arrested Unal Ustel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), said the ship’s captain and seven crew members had been arrested. The TRNC, which is recognised only by Turkiye, controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974. The territory is served with regular air and sea links to Turkiye. The TRNC’s transport minister Erhan Arikli said the ferry had “completely sunk to a depth of 514 metres (1,686 feet)”. “Efforts to find the missing are continuing tirelessly,” Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said during a public ceremony. “We hope to receive positive news from these efforts.” The TRNC is dependent on Turkiye, and Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said on X: “We are providing all necessary assistance to the search and rescue operations.” One rescued passenger who spoke of a blast on board told local TRNC television after he was taken back ashore: “The front part exploded, they tried to turn around. And the side windows blew out. The boat started taking on water.” The man, aged in his 50s and not named, said he spent an hour and a half in the water before being rescued. He said many people had been inside the ferry when it started taking on water. “Those who could, got out,” he said, adding that he saw the captain among the first to abandon ship “without organising anything”. Another witness, in his thirties, corroborated reports of an explosion. He said he had reported water leaks to the captain. “The seats started to float, the captain kept going, and the bow exploded,” he said. Many inside Many boats, including private ones, were involved in the rescue operation. Turkiye’s interior ministry said on X that six Turkish navy ships had also been dispatched. “All necessary preparations are being made for a swift response from rescue and health services,” the TRNC’s health ministry said in a statement. Hospitals in the territory had been alerted, to provide any needed medical attention, it added. Pakistan extends condolences Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Deputy PM Ishaq Dar both said they were “deeply saddened by the tragic” incident in the Mediterranean Sea. “I extend my heartfelt condolences to my dear brother President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, the Turkish government and the bereaved families,” PM Shehbaz wrote on X. He prayed for the swift and safe recovery of those missing, affirming that the people of Pakistan stood in solidarity with the Turkish nation “at this difficult time”. Expressing his condolences to the families of those who lost their lives, Dar wrote, “Our thoughts and prayers are with all those affected and with the missing persons and their loved ones.” He also prayed for the success of search and rescue operations.

Trump says NBC journalist should face 'punishment' from broadcast regulator. United States President Donald Trump on Sunday threatened a prominent NBC broadcast journalist with possible punishment by US media regulators as the Republican expressed disappointment with coverage of his candidate endorsements ahead of November’s midterm elections. Trump took to his Truth Social platform to attack Kristen Welker as the “unpopular ‘hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press” talk show. He objected to her having said the president had had “mixed results” on his endorsement of political candidates in party primaries, insisting the races had gone his way 98 per cent to 100pc of the time. Welker, speaking early Sunday to a local NBC affiliate, said Trump would “loom large over these midterms”. When it came to endorsements, she added, he “had some mixed results, but most recently, his pick of Senator Darline Graham… was successful in her primary battle”. Trump, in his comments, said that “because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment”. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) assigns and oversees licenses for radio and television broadcast frequencies. “Unfortunately, she is not the only one,” he added. “The Radical Left News is going out of their way to harass, demean, and libel anything ‘TRUMP’.” Welker is an award-winning journalist who earned bipartisan praise after moderating a 2020 presidential debate featuring Trump and Joe Biden, the Democrat who won that year’s election. An NBC News spokesperson, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, defended Welker on Sunday, telling AFP that “Kristen is one of the best in the business and we stand by her”. Billionaire Trump used American media to his advantage over the years as a provocative real estate developer in New York. But as president he dramatically turned against the press and what he called “fake news”. He has sued several newspapers including the Wall Street Journal and New York Times , and ordered federal funding slashed for public media. His administration has ramped up restrictions and attempts to intimidate journalists, and the FCC — headed by a close Trump associate — has pressured broadcasters to toe the line. “I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” Trump said. The latest attack is part of the Trump administration’s months-long offensive against media outlets it deems overly critical. Such efforts are facing growing resistance from news organisations and major broadcast networks. Several of them have filed lawsuits against the FCC, arguing such pressure constitutes political retaliation that violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which protects freedom of speech. Relations between Trump and Welker have been under pressure for months. In June, the president abruptly cut short an interview with her following a tense exchange, during which he grew irritated by Welker’s questioning, particularly on the war against Iran. Experts argue the FCC lacks the legal authority to punish broadcasters or reporters for their viewpoints. According to a 2025 paper by the Yale Journal on Regulation, the US Supreme Court has confirmed that US law “does not grant the FCC the power to ban controversial speech”.

Health minister opposes ‘permanent’ staff in public sector hospitals. • Mustafa Kamal says not minister’s job to manage a hospital; says elected mayor or his team should be looking after Pims affairs • Suggests bringing in CEO from private sector; all hirings on contract, performance-basis • New Pims ED takes charge, vows to prioritise patient safety ISLAMABAD: Days after a tragic fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) claimed the lives of 14 newborn babies, Health Minister Mustafa Kamal seemingly stirred another hornet’s nest by suggesting that there should be no permanent employees at government-run hospitals. “There should be no permanent government scale employees in hospitals, they should all be employed on contract basis, and a CEO should be brought in from the private sector to run things effectively,” Mr Kamal said during an interview with Geo News on Sunday night. Lamenting that permanent employees were extremely powerful and embroiled their departments in litigation if they were ever dismissed, Mr Kamal touted his idea as the only ‘permanent solution’ to the prevailing rot in the country’s healthcare system. “Whoever performs and works should remain, everyone else should be let got. A CEO should be brought in [from the private sector] who should have full hiring-and-firing authority. They should get their annual budget approved from us and then be responsible for managing their affairs and ensuring accountability,” he said. Mr Kamal also noted that the inquiry report into the deadly fire in the gynae ward had found that only 120 seconds, or two minutes, elapsed between the first spark and the fire engulfing the entire Mother and Child Health Centre. When asked about a fire that had broken out in a Pims nursing hostel around a month ago, the health minister said he had only learnt of the incident after last week’s tragedy. He explained that at the time, a bulb in the waiting room of the nurse’s hostel had short-circuited and fell onto a sofa, which caught fire. He maintained that this incident was not reported to the ministry at any level, nor was it a major incident of the kind that would have been reported by the media. However, he maintained that the previous executive director (ED) had internally formed a committee to conduct an inquiry and provide a way forward. The report of that committee, he said, was only submitted to the ED just a day prior to last week’s tragedy. Referring to reports that he had already offered his resignation to PM Shehbaz, but was asked to hold off until the investigation into the incident concluded, Mr Kamal said the ministerial slot did not hold any meaning for him. He recalled how he had taken responsibility on the floor of the National Assembly. “When I am offering myself up for accountability, then no one should be spared… even though I am not at fault in any of this, but I do take responsibility as the minister,” he said. When asked about criticism against him and calls for his resignation – especially from the PPP – Mr Kamal regretted how the party was trying to link this to the issue of new administrative units, at a time when such a tragedy had taken place. However, Mr Kamal insisted that what transpired actually supports his viewpoint on the issue of new provinces . “If Islamabad were a separate administrative unit, with elected officials and a mayor who was directly elected by the people, they should be the ones tasked with running this hospital,” he said. Maintaining that he had to focus on larger issues, such as the country’s health policy, Mr Kamal insisted: “It should not be a minister’s job to run a hospital; it should be under an elected mayor”. To a question, he said that the new ED — who is the CEO of the National Institute of Health, Islamabad, had been appointed on the recommendation of the inquiry committee. He regretted that many of the top officials at such institutions considered themselves ‘kings’, since they were assured of the fact that no outsider could be brought in to take their place. “The new ED has been appointed after relaxing the rules; in principle no one can be brought in from outside… now we need post-facto cabinet approval for [the new ED’s appointment]. New ED takes charge Earlier, speaking to reporters after taking charge on Sunday, new Pims ED Dr Muhammad Salman said that patient safety would be his top priority. After taking charge of his post, Dr Salman visited different departments at the hospital and inspected arrangements in place. He also called a meeting of the heads of different departments and discussed the prevailing situation with them. Talking to media persons, he said : “Although it is a challenging situation but as responsibility has been given to me, I will try to prove myself. We will implement the recommendations of the inquiry committee and priority will be to ensure patient safety. The short term objective is to ensure that such incidents would not be repeated in future,” he said. Dr Salman said that other hazards will also be looked at. “There is heavy patient load on the hospital so it will also be managed. Referral system will also be made stronger so that the patient management would improve,” he said. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

Central Development Working Party clears five projects worth over Rs60 billion. • Plans include Gwadar water scheme, Karachi neighbourhood project, Gilgit medical college, NDU campus and Orakzai road • Study on wastewater treatment in Gwadar ordered to prevent sewage from polluting sea ISLAMABAD: The Central Development Working Party (CDWP) has cleared five development projects involving an estimated cost of over Rs60 billion, including a multi-billion-rupee water supply project to provide water from Mirani Dam to Gwadar through a 125-kilometre pipeline. The CDWP meeting, presided over by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, approved three development projects with a combined estimated cost of Rs11.7bn. It recommended two other projects worth Rs48.545bn for approval by the Executive Com­mittee of the National Economic Council (Ecnec), including the procedural clearance of the Rs19.55bn Karachi Neighbourhood Impro­vement Project (KNIP), which is already nearing completion with a World Bank loan. Under the current financial rules approved by the National Economic Council (NEC), the CDWP is empowered to approve projects costing up to Rs7.5bn, while projects with higher estimated costs are approved by Ecnec on the recommendations of the CDWP after technical clearance. Based on a technical evaluation by the Planning Commission, the CDWP recommended reducing the estimated cost of the “Construction of Water Supply Scheme to Gwadar Town from Mirani Dam under Balochistan Socio-Economic Deve­lopment Projects Phase-III” by around 20 per cent to Rs23.82bn, against the Rs29bn proposed by the Balochistan government. The reduction would result in an estimated saving of Rs5.235bn without any change in the design or scope of the project. The Planning Commission rationalised the project cost by 20 per cent, exclusively under non-scheduled items, which account for approximately Rs23.4bn, or 86.7pc, of the base cost, by curtailing contractor overheads. It has, however, asked Ecnec to approve the project subject to satisfactory resolution of outstanding technical observations, particularly regarding demand figures, hydrology, confirmation of the water source, procurement strategy, land acquisition status, a self-sustainable operation and maintenance (O&M) strategy, and a realistic implementation plan. While reviewing the project, Minister Ahsan Iqbal directed the provincial government to initiate a study on wastewater treatment in Gwadar, observing that the city should not be allowed to become another Karachi, with sewage polluting the sea. He also allowed the project to proceed to the bidding stage to save time, but directed that the contract should not be awarded until the project receives approval from Ecnec. The CDWP also cleared the “Karachi Neighbourhood Impro­vement Project”, with a revised cost of Rs19.55bn, for approval by Ecnec. The project is proposed to be financed through foreign funding, including an $85 million (Rs16.7bn) World Bank loan and Rs2.8bn contributions from the Sindh government. While discussing the Karachi project, the CDWP constituted a committee comprising the Planning Commission’s member (Population), member (Infrastructure) and a representative of the Economic Affairs Division (EAD) to develop a comprehensive framework for effective monitoring, transparency and accountability of foreign-funded development projects. Of the three smaller projects, with a combined estimated cost of Rs11.714bn, the CDWP approved the establishment of a Medical and Nursing College at Gilgit at an estimated cost of Rs4.924bn. The CDWP also approved the establishment of a National Defence University (NDU) FCS Campus at Defence Complex Islamabad (DCI) at an estimated cost of Rs2.75bn. It also approved the “Construction of Road from Zera to Daboori, District Orakzai (53.4 km)” at a cost of Rs4.037bn. The minister directed that funds be released before the winter season to facilitate completion of the project, which has been lingering since 2016. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

Nasa launches new telescope to map cosmos. SPACEX launches Roman on a Falcon Heavy rocket from Nasa’s Kennedy Space Centre in Florida.—X/SpaceX • Roman designed to shed light on ‘unsolved mysteries’ including dark matter and dark energy • Also aims to discover thousands of exoplanets and supernovae • With its infrared vision, telescope will be able to detect light emitted by celestial objects billions of years ago WASHINGTON: Nasa laun­ched its new flagship space telescope on Sunday, embarking on a multi-year mission to create an unprecedented map of the cosmos and shed light on some of the biggest mysteries in physics. Designed to take a panoramic view of the vast reaches of space, the Roman Space Telescope “will help unlock the secrets of the universe”, US President Donald Trump said on Friday during a ceremony at Nasa headquarters in Houston, Texas. Standing over 12 metres (39 feet) tall, the state-of-the-art observatory launched from the Kennedy Space Centre in Florida aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. Developed over more than a decade at a cost topping $4 billion, the telescope is named after pioneering US astronomer Nancy Grace Roman, who became known as the “Mother of Hubble”, another of Nasa’s flagship telescopes. While Hubble revealed that the universe is expanding faster than previously thought, Roman will seek to answer some of the other unsolved mysteries, including those of dark matter and dark energy. “Roman will give the Earth a new atlas of the universe,” Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman said in April when he unveiled the project to the press. Studying the invisible With a field of view more than 100 times larger than Hubble’s — and significantly wider than James Webb’s — Roman will survey vast swaths of the sky from a vantage point 1.5 million kilometres (930,000 miles) from Earth, which it will take about 100 days to reach. Designed to work in tandem with other observatories such as Webb, which offers greater power and precision, Roman aims to discover thousands of exoplanets as well as tens of thousands of supernovae, the explosive deaths of massive stars. “It will be the biggest catalog of astronomical objects anybody’s ever produced, and it will help us understand how common are solar systems like our own,” Dave Content, Roman’s technical manager, told AFP. The new telescope will also shed light on two of the biggest mysteries in physics: dark matter and dark energy. Their origins remain unknown, but together they are believed to make up about 95 per cent of the universe. Dark matter is thought to act as a kind of gravitational glue, while dark energy is believed to be a repulsive force driving the universe’s expansion. With its infrared vision, Roman will be able to detect light emitted by celestial objects billions of years ago, effectively looking back in time and offering scientists a glimpse into the universe’s distant past and helping them better understand these two mysterious phenomena. Roman’s observations will complement the work of the Rubin Observatory in Chile and the European Space Agency’s Euclid probe, and are highly anticipated because they could challenge scientists’ understanding of the universe’s structure. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

Punjab moves to prevent Pims-like tragedies. • Orders Rescue 1122 deployment at all teaching hospitals across the province • 11-member working group to prepare SOPs for nursery, neonatology units LAHORE: The Punjab government has initiated multiple major steps at public-sector hospitals across the province to prevent a recurrence of the incident that clai­med the lives of 14 infants at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) in Islamabad. The Specialised Healthcare & Medical Education Department on Sunday asked Emergency Services Department (ESD) Pu­n­­jab Secretary Rizwan Naseer to dep­loy Rescue 1122 officials at all government teaching hospitals across the province. Through an official letter, the health secretary apprised the ESD head that it had been decided to engage the services of Punjab Emergency Service Rescue 1122 to establish a uniform and standard emergency response mechanism and strengthen emergency preparedness, response and coordination at tertiary-care hospitals across Punjab. He said the main objective of the initiative was to establish a robust, integrated and uniform emergency response system with clearly defined roles, a command structure and escalation mechanisms across all tertiary-care hospitals. “Emergency officers will be responsible for standardising and monitoring emergency response protocols,” the letter stated, adding that the officers would coordinate with hospital emergency, security, fire-safety and other relevant teams. They would also be responsible for conducting regular inspections of emergency exits, fire extinguishers and life-safety arrangements. The health secretary also sought the names, designations and contact details of the officers to be app­ointed at the hospitals to discharge the assigned responsibilities. Technical Working Group Separately, the Punjab government has constituted an 11-member Technical Working Group (TWG), comprising senior medical teachers and doctors, to review and prepare Standard Operating Proce­dures (SOPs) for nursery and neonatology setups at all public-sector teaching hospitals in the province. A notification in this regard was issued, appointing University of Child Health Sciences Lahore Vice Chancellor Prof Masood Sadiq as its convener. According to its terms of reference, the committee shall develop clinical admission and discharge criteria to optimise utilisation and load management; establish formal step-down and shared-care pathways with peripheral hospitals to divert stable neonates for efficient utilisation of available resources; and guide hospitals on infrastructure requirements relating to fire hazards, electrical-load risks and evacuation challenges. Similarly, the committee shall draft comprehensive SOPs for fire safety, evacuation, firefighting and electrical-load management tailored to neonatal settings; design training modules for doctors, nurses and support staff on evacuation drills, neonatal handling and basic firefighting; and develop checklists and audit tools for regular compliance monitoring. The committee has been directed to submit its recommendations to the competent authority within seven days. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

Six months on. IT has been six months since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran — a costly misadventure that remains far from being resolved. In fact, the threat of renewed hostilities is ever-present, despite efforts by regional states, such as Pakistan , Oman and Qatar , to revive peace talks. The war has been a miscalculation of Trumpian proportions, and the US president and his coterie of war hawks have few ‘good’ options to save face and bring their troops home. Despite the decimation of its religious, political and military top tier in the first few days of the conflict, Iran — which is militarily no match for the US war machine — managed to defend itself, and now conservative factions within the Iranian establishment are unwilling to back down. Rather, they seem prepared to absorb the pain and play the long game with the Americans. Yet instead of realising that the kinetic option has failed against Tehran, the US has stepped up its economic war against the Islamic Republic, warning sovereign states not to do business with Iran. While this action will impact the Iranian economy — which has survived sanctions for over four decades — it is unlikely to make Tehran raise the white flag, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying, “pressure doesn’t work”. Moreover, China, the world’s second biggest economy and a major trading partner of Iran, is not buying it . As the Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said, Beijing “opposes illegal, unilateral sanctions”. Just as the US failed to defeat Iran on the battlefield, it may also fail on the economic front. Wise nations learn from mistakes. But while wisdom may admittedly be in short supply in the White House at the moment, it is time the US put aside its ego and committed itself to finding a diplomatic solution with Iran. The nuclear issue consists of hype more than any credible Iranian threat, while the Strait of Hormuz blockade by Iran is a direct result of the US aggression, with Tehran using the key waterway as a bargaining chip to secure its interests and security. The Islamabad MoU continues to offer the best available off-ramp to all sides, and both Washington and Tehran should return to the spirit of this document. The Iranian president has reaffirmed his country’s belief in dialogue; it is time President Donald Trump did the same. Instead of playing global policeman, the US should re-evaluate its role in the Middle East. Let regional states — specifically Iran and the Arabs — reach a mutually acceptable security framework. If there is to be long-term peace in the region, the US and Israel must end their armed aggression against sovereign states, and allow the people of the region to work out solutions amongst themselves. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

Filling in the connectivity puzzle. For all the progress Pakistan has made in expanding internet access, the coverage is still anything but reliable. Forget the mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan or the Thar desert; just try driving to the outskirts of a metropolis and see signal bars disappear on your phone. Ask any operator about it and they would, justifiably so, start a monologue about the underlying reasons. But with satellite, the whole connectivity landscape can change as billionaires (or trillionaires?) pour their money into expanding the technology. To understand whether they can truly scale, let’s first get a sense of how connected Pakistan is currently. By the end of FY26, the country had roughly 164 million broadband connections, of which an overwhelming majority — 159.5m — were via mobile data. Fixed makes up just 4.4m, roughly a tenth of all households. Within this smaller base, all focus lately has naturally been towards fibre, which has grown from around 100,000 connections in FY19 to 2.88m by June. While the rate of uptake is impressive, the sheer scale is still quite sobering, as under 8pc of households are fiberised. The problem is economics: laying fibre to a single home runs somewhere between Rs60,000 and Rs120,000, with most of the core inputs — the cable, optical network terminals, splitters — almost entirely imported, then hit with tariffs of around 70 per cent on top. The customer, though, pays only a small fraction, some Rs10,000-15,000 upfront. The internet service provider (ISP) must bear this capex, extending the payback period to eight or 10 years. The math only works where incomes and population density cross a certain threshold, which typically happens to be the same urban neighbourhoods already connected. In relatively remote geographies, mobile connectivity — let alone fixed — remains patchy still. For now, satellite broadband has limited ability to help bridge the connectivity gaps Since satellite terminals, by design, cater to a static location, they are sort of an alternative to fixed broadband. Both cater to non-individual use cases and usually offer higher speeds, and unlike fibre, this doesn’t require you to wait for an ISP to lay out a cable. While the technology continues to evolve, it faces two general constraints. First, satellite is slower than a wired connection — a matter of simple physics because the signal has further to travel — though in Pakistan you could well find fibre lagging behind not just satellite but even a good mobile connection. Secondly, in most markets it still costs more than what an average, or even well-off, household pays for a fixed line, even if that gap is narrowing. So where does it make the most sense to go for satellite instead? A few segments stand out. First are the connectivity deserts — Balochistan, upper Gilgit-Baltistan, the low-density districts where neither fibre nor a tower will make much sense — served either through Universal Service Fund subsidies or community leaders sharing a dish or two across a certain radius. Then come enterprise and continuity users, from remote offices still on VSAT (very small aperture terminal) links to premium urban households wanting a backup connection. There is also backhaul for remote towers: fewer than 18pc of Pakistan’s roughly 60,000 cellular sites are fiberised, a figure meant to reach just 35pc by 2032. And finally, the most niche of all, disaster response and mobility — floods, aviation, maritime — where the connection must survive an outage or travel with the user. Luckily, you don’t have to take my word for it, as we can learn from comparable markets that have already run the experiment. Nigeria is considered one of Starlink’s emerging-market successes, reaching around 92,000 customers by March 2026, with demand outpacing capacity in Lagos and Abuja to the point that signups were frozen and thousands pushed onto waitlists. Bangladesh sits in the opposite corner: nine months after launch, it had just 3,990 subscribers against a fixed-broadband base of roughly 14.5m, despite effectively rolling out a red carpet for satellite connectivity. That begs the question: what really predicts uptake of LEO (low Earth orbit)? We analysed a global panel, taking each technology as a share of households. Once you control for income, fibre and satellite tend to act as substitutes, though the effect holds only in poorer and middle-income countries and disappears among the rich. For incumbents, this poses interesting choices. Fixed-line ISPs face a possible substitution effect at the top end, since Pakistan ranks 143rd out of 149 countries on median fixed broadband speed, at a dismal 18.21 Mbps (megabits per second), compared with 125.59 Mbps globally. There is surely a segment tired of what it is currently getting, but how big is it? Under 4.7pc of all fixed connections have advertised speeds above 30 Mbps and not even 0.5pc above 100 Mbps — roughly 215,000 connections, under 5pc of the fixed base. Not much of a market, and urban density would complicate even that. Mobile operators, by contrast, might not face a serious direct threat, since the two go for different use cases. The real squeeze could fall on the GEO (geostationary Earth orbit)/VSAT layer, the PTCL Skylinks and Supernets, which serve exactly the enterprise, remote-site and continuity accounts satellite is built to take. To be fair, it was never a mass-market play to begin with. For now, the case for satellite rests on the state of technology as of today. But satellite is moving fast: launch costs keep falling, each new constellation adds capacity, and competitors like Kuiper are only starting to come online. None of that changes the basic logic, which is that satellite is a complement rather than a replacement. What it does change is the size of that complement, which is likely to grow. The question for Pakistan isn’t if there are large, even if not truly mass, use cases for satellite. It’s whether the regulation, the infrastructure and the pricing move fast enough to let it. Abdul Aziz Malik is an ex analyst at Data Darbar and Mutaher Khan is co-founder of Data Darbar Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, August 31st, 2026

Gul Plaza fire commission blames no single entity or person directly. KARACHI: Deploring the failure to transform available resources into effective and coordinated firefighting and rescue efforts, the Gul Plaza Judicial Commission in its report says that the deadly inferno has signified a systemic failure across successive provincial and local governments as the legal and administrative mechanisms have existed, but could not be implemented effectively. The report of the commission, headed by Justice Agha Faisal of the Sindh High Court, was handed over to the provincial government months ago but authorities preferred not to make it public. However, the report, which bore no signatures, was silently released on Saturday apparently against the backdrop of the tragic incident at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), Islamabad. In the report, Justice Agha Faisal notes that the tragic incident was a grave indictment of the failure of municipal and provincial systems to translate legal duties concerning urban safety into effective protection on the ground. In his report, Justice Agha Faisal says ‘sustained underperformance by public systems’ caused the tragedy; highlights failures of municipal and provincial systems It also states that the people have not only lost their lives to flames, but also due to delay, darkness, locked exits and windows of the ill-fated building, absence of fire safety systems, unimplemented audits/inspections and fragmented authority. The commission further says that Karachi Metropolitan Corporation, including its fire brigade, Sindh Building Control Authority, Rescue 1122, civil defence department, district administration and others bear institutional responsibilities for failure while material responsibility rested with the people acting as the de facto management of the building together with owners, occupants and commercial operators. It says holistically, the evidence suggested that the prevailing administrative and emergency response set-up did not appear to be adequately trained, coordinated or equipped to deal with an incident of such magnitude. Over 70 people had lost their lives in the devastating fire which had erupted on the night of Jan 17 and took nearly two days to be fully extinguished, leaving the ground-plus-three-storey building of Gul Plaza in ruins, with some of its sections collapsed. The Sindh government had constituted the judicial commission in February to investigate the deadly fire incident and to fix responsibility of any acts of commission or omission committed prior and subsequent to the incident. After conducting the probe, the commission had handed over the sealed inquiry report along with the entire record to the secretary law department in April. The 78-page inquiry report of the commission, issued by the home department, says that the systemic conclusion did not exonerate the institutions concerned nor did it single out the current period alone and instead the commission recognises that the tragedy was the human cost of sustained underperformance by public systems meant to protect life. “When a large commercial building remains unsafe despite known deficiencies, when audits do not result in compliance, when the building-control record is incomplete, when coordination structures remain on paper, and when rescue is attempted without fully exploiting available opportunities, the eventual loss is not merely accidental. It becomes the foreseeable product of systemic failure”, it adds. The commission’s report also states that the failure was not only limited to one department or building, but it was cumulative, layered and institutional as mechanisms, audit/building-control powers, firefighting obligations, emergency response structures and court-backed coordination framework had existed, but could not be implemented and the system did not function as a system. It further points out that the condition of the plaza, the opacity and incompleteness of its building-control history, absence of reliable inspection material at the stage of amnesty and regularisation, the persistence of audit non-compliance, the failure of coordinated enforcement and weakness of the emergency-support environment reflected a cumulative failure across successive provincial and local governments. “The commission does not make this observation to diffuse present responsibility. It makes it because the institutional truth of this case demands it. The risk at Gul Plaza accumulated over time because municipal and provincial structures, across successive periods, did not evolve or function in a manner commensurate with the hazards of dense commercial urban development”, it adds. The inquiry report says: “At the highest level, the case represents a systemic failure across successive provincial and local governments, in which legal and administrative mechanisms existed but were not effectively implemented.” The commission holds that the tragedy resulted from a convergence of known and unrectified hazards, inadequate managerial judgement, ineffective enforcement, fragmented institutional coordination, delayed and constrained emergency response and a system that failed to function as an effective whole. “The disaster was not merely the consequence of a fire. It was the consequence of a building left unsafe, warnings left unimplemented, authority left unexercised, and rescue opportunities left insufficiently exploited until irreversible loss followed”, it adds. It also says, “Therefore, those who perished in Gul Plaza Inferno were lost not only to flame. They were lost to delay, to darkness, to locked exits, to blocked windows, to absent systems, to unimplemented audits, to fragmented authority, and to a civic order that did not protect them in time. The present case is a grave indictment of the failure of municipal and provincial systems, over time, to translate legal duties concerning urban safety into effective protection on the ground”. Regarding the question of ignition, the material placed before the commission indicated a consistent and unrebutted position as the SSP (South) in his response confirmed the cause of fire because of children playing with and igniting matchsticks at shop No.193 in the plaza, and such fact has also been confirmed by an inquiry report of the commissioner of Karachi.
