Another failed strategy?. PRESIDENT Donald Trump’s declaration of economic war on Iran is likely to backfire just like his bombing campaign failed to force Iran to surrender. It also exposed the limits of US military options. Wrapped in hyperbolic language, his threats to impose the “toughest sanctions in history” and “the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country” were met with defiance by Tehran. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed them, saying “We have seen this movie before”. Iranian officials warned of halting all oil flows from the Gulf and delivering an “earthquake-like” retaliation if Washington followed through. On what US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Economic D-Day last week, he announced measures to sever Iran’s “financial lifelines” and force a “regime endgame”. But earlier, Trump telephoned Pakistan’s chief of defence forces, Field Marshal Asim Munir and asked him to persuade Iran to resume negotiations. FM Munir then headed to Tehran for talks with Iranian leaders. For all his blusterous rhetoric about “crippling Iran” the outreach was another sign of Trump’s desperation for a deal to end the six-month-old conflict. His flailing actions showed his growing frustration with a deeply unpopular war in his country. According to officials, Pakistan urged Trump to allow time for diplomacy to produce results. Even as mediation efforts got underway, the Trump administration went ahead with the announcement to ratchet up “unprecedented” pressure on Iran and compel it to return to the negotiating table. Iranian officials responded by saying they were “fully prepared” to counter the sanctions, which were an “act of state and economic terrorism”. Bessent widened the scope of economic sanctions against Iran but offered few details of what he called ‘Operation Economic Outcast’. Sanctions targeted Iran’s digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors. It involved action against 60 entities, individuals and vessels. Alongside the financial measures Treasury Secretary Bessent warned the US would punish and isolate countries that continued to trade with Iran and had dealings with its financial system. His ‘either you are with us or against us’ mantra had a wearingly familiar ring. Trump had already issued the same ultimatum, threatening economic penalties against any country doing business with Iran. Tehran responded in kind. It warned that any state, including its neighbours, that joined US economic warfare would be treated as “an enemy”. Trump’s economic warfare will be as futile as his bombing campaign to force Iran to surrender. Bessent said Trump would be phoning some world leaders to ask them to cease their financial interactions with Tehran. But he named no target countries for secondary sanctions. Nor did he say what the penalties would be or specify any timeline for enforcement. No immediate action was taken against Iran’s biggest trading partners. That suggested that the door to de-escalation was being kept open. In any case, it was hardly the first time the tool of sanctions was deployed. Iran has been under multiple US sanctions for four decades and survived them. It seems ready to absorb the pain from this round too. It was also not the first time Trump targeted Iran’s trading partners. Before the war began, he announced tariffs on countries with business ties to Iran. The plan fizzled out and was soon overtaken by the US-Israeli military assault on Iran. For now, only the UAE has declared a halt to trade and financial transactions with Iran. This was before Bessent’s announcement and ostensibly in response to ballistic missiles being fired at it, which Iran denied. The suspension will add to Iran’s troubles with its fragile economy facing high inflation and a weakening currency. But it is unclear how and the extent to which the Emirati decision will be enforced. Qatar described US sanctions as unilateral and called instead for mediation efforts. The US depends on the cooperation of other nations to achieve the goals of its punitive economic campaign. China has already pushed back saying pressure tactics won’t work. After Bessent’s threat, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesman said China “will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own interests” from “illegal unilateral sanctions”. Beijing warned of retaliation if the US imposes secondary sanctions. Washington is unlikely to go beyond threats and want a showdown with its biggest trading partner, especially with a Trump-President Xi Jinping summit coming up next month in Washington. Too much is at stake in that relationship to risk that. The US expectation that countries will fall in line assumes they will give preference to ingratiating themselves with Washington over their own economic interests. This will turn out to be another miscalculation. Many analysts also see it as unsustainable and resting on mistaken assumptions. As Robert Kagan writes in The Atlantic , “nations that depend on access to the strait — Japan and South Korea, for example — will have to choose between access to a reliable energy supply and participation in American-backed sanctions”. It is improbable they will choose solidarity with Trump’s Washington over their economic interests. He also points out that “the idea that, having survived both military strikes and sanctions, Iran will now succumb to sanctions alone is deluded”. At the same time, mediation efforts by Pakistan and Gulf countries are intensifying and making headway, according to credible reports. This suggests the warring sides haven’t given up on diplomacy. Behind the tough rhetoric of both countries, backchannel communication is aimed at getting negotiations restarted. Tehran wants the US to affirm and abide by the Memorandum of Understanding. Trump wants the Strait of Hormuz to reopen. Iran is reportedly preparing to submit its conditions for reopening the strategic waterway to mediators. The regional mediation initiative aims to first secure a ceasefire, followed by the prompt reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the termination of the US blockade. Whether this can be achieved in coming days remains to be seen. What seems clear is that Trump’s hope that America’s financial muscle will give him victory over Iran will prove to be as futile as his use of military might. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

New units. THE debate on new provinces rests on two different levels. The first is the broader technocratic concern with decentralisation and its hypothetical impact on social welfare and economic growth outcomes. The second is the political economy of constitutional and administrative reform in divided polities. Both aspects are important and it is revealing which one is highlighted by whom and at what point. Let’s start with the first one. Recent research presents a nuanced, but positive leaning relationship between decentralisation reforms and human development/welfare outcomes. In an influential 2016 review article, Channa and Faguet found that decentralisation of health and education spending tends to improve sectoral outcomes, thou­­gh quality of evidence varies considerably across different cases. Miranda-Lescano et al. (2023) found that decentralising subnational government spending (especially health) positively affects HDI across 57 countries (2000-18). They argue further that such welfare/HDI effects have been understudied relative to growth and governance. The key here is the type of decentralisation that takes place. Reviews of the fiscal decentralisation literature (such as Canare 2021) suggest that revenue decentralisation and fiscal independence, ie, local governments’ ability to raise their own revenue rather than depend on central transfers, are most consistently associated with better development outcomes, while expenditure decentralisation shows no clear pattern. On a cautionary note, there is some evidence to suggest that in weakly governed contexts, usually characterised by low levels of bureaucratic efficiency and transparency, the proliferation of administrative units may also hamper developmental processes, including those associated with economic growth. The discourse in Pakistan needs to take cognisance of what it hopes to primarily achieve through decentralisation. Overall, the picture that emerges is that the right type of decentralisation varies by country, though once in place, it can lead to important gains in development. For a context like Pakistan, the right type of decentralisation would necessarily include not just administrative devolution, but also fiscal devolution. Local governments at whatever tier they work should have the ability to raise revenue and control expenditure, including expenditure on human resource (ie, bureaucrats and other public sector workers). The discourse in Pakistan, regulated as it is from the top down, has fluctuated between re­­­wo­r­­king provincial boundaries or elevating divisions as ‘administrative units’ with expanded control over various governance aspects. What it is unable to do in clear terms is establish the clear case behind why devolution is needed at this stage. If the primary impetus is to improve social welfare/human development outcomes (ie, outcomes in health and school education), then we may have to come up with a distinct form of devolution. If the impetus is to enable more productive use of capital and labour (ie, catalyse economic growth and transformation), the system that comes out might end up looking a lot different. For more effective human development, Evans and Heller (2015) make an important argument that states require a greater degree of embeddedness with disadvantaged groups in order to deliver the type of welfare gains needed by them. In other words, this means a form of decentralisation that is accountable and participatory at the local level, and one that can avoid the pitfall of local elite capture by propertied groups or by unaccountable bureaucrats. Alternatively, for catalysing economic outcomes, East Asia’s experience suggests that close ties between state and capital, along with high levels of bureaucratic efficiency and autonomy, are necessary to deliver higher rates of growth. China’s decentralisation in the contemporary era, for example, is not necessarily built for the expansion of human capabilities, but rather guiding local capital, and thus it takes a very different form altogether. The discourse in Pakistan (that pitches technocratic reform) needs to take cognisance of what it hopes to primarily achieve through decentralisation. The form of decentralisation and the requisite level that it would have to be aimed at would then flow from this first clarity. In the present it appears the urge for new provinces or even elevating divisions to some as yet unspecified form of administrative unit is driven by political exigency rather than a purpose-led attempt to reform governance. This brings us to the second level of the issue, which is the political economy of reform. The opposition to new provinces or related administrative rejigging rests on both identity-based but also political grounds. Sindhi nationalists speak about the dilution of Sindhi identity and the denial of resources if Karachi is separated. PTI leaders talk about the questionable mandate of the government to undertake a step of this nature. Both of these are not some exceptional or unique forms of opposition. Ethnolinguistic nationalism is an oppositional force in this country as it is in many others. While I personally don’t see how the creation of new administrative units (without any demographic change) can dilute a linguistic identity, it remains a popular position in Sindh and one that has to be reckoned with through politics. The PTI’s response also appears quite decisive in this instance. Change that is introduced under questionable conditions, and with limited legitimacy to back it, is precarious and transient. This is exactly what has plagued previous attempts at de­­­volution or admin reconfiguration, including the 2001 local government ordinance. Ultimately, po­­p­­ular opposition to the manner of implementation makes a worthwhile idea seem worthless as well. The reversal of local governments happened because while they were popular with citizens and local political workers, it was very easy to paint them as the illegitimate engineering attempts of a dictator. Under this reasoning, provincial political elites were able to cement their own type of governing arrangement and recreate centralised rule in the provinces. A similar risk is posed if large-scale administrative change is pushed both without purpose-led clarity and in the face of popular opposition. Fiscally empowered local governments under the provinces, with reasonable judicial or even constitutional protections, might be the most appropriate concession at this stage. And one that may prove to be more sustainable even after the incumbent regime exits. The writer teaches politics and sociology at Lums. X: @umairjav Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

Developing the battery recycling industry. For entrepreneurs considering Pakistan’s emerging lithium-ion battery recycling industry, the first question is usually straightforward: how much capital is required? The answer is less straightforward. There is no single price tag for entering battery recycling because recycling is not one business. It is a chain of activities ranging from collection and dismantling to mechanical processing and sophisticated chemical recovery. The amount of capital required depends largely on where an investor chooses to enter that chain. This distinction is particularly important for Pakistan. The image of battery recycling as a large chemical plant requiring hundreds of millions of dollars can discourage smaller investors from exploring the sector. In reality, businesses can enter at considerably different levels of technical and financial complexity. The first level is collection, sorting, diagnostics and dismantling. Used batteries must be collected from households, solar installations, electric vehicles, telecommunications systems and industrial users before they can be recycled. They then need to be identified by chemical analysis, tested, safely discharged, and assessed for reuse or recycling. Beginning at the lower and middle parts of the chain may offer a more realistic route to investing in this sector This represents the lowest-capital entry point. Investment is primarily required for secure storage, diagnostic and discharge equipment, insulated tools, fire protection, material-handling systems and safe transportation. The business model can generate revenues through collection contracts, resale of reusable batteries, second-life applications and supplying sorted batteries to larger recycling facilities. The second level is mechanical processing. Here the investment becomes significantly larger. Batteries are discharged and dismantled before cells are shredded in controlled conditions. Mechanical separation then recovers materials such as copper, aluminium, steel and plastics while producing black mass containing the battery’s active materials. International estimates illustrate the difference in scale. A technical business case prepared by South Africa’s Mintek estimated capital expenditure of approximately $180,000 for a 100-tonne-per-year black-mass processing operation. Increasing capacity to 9,000 tonnes per year raised estimated capital expenditure to around $3.5 million. These figures are international engineering estimates rather than quotations for Pakistan, but they demonstrate that mechanical processing can provide an intermediate route between small-scale dismantling and full chemical refining. The third level involves recovering metals from black mass. Hydrometallurgical facilities use chemical processes to recover lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and other materials. They require reactors, filtration and separation systems, chemical storage, laboratories, wastewater treatment and environmental controls. The same international study estimated capital expenditure of approximately $660,000 for a 100-tonne-per-year hydrometallurgical facility, increasing to around $12.3 million at 9,000 tonnes annually. Pyrometallurgical processing, which relies on high-temperature treatment, was estimated at approximately $1.06m at 100 tonnes and $20.7m at 9,000 tonnes per year. Again, these should be treated as international benchmarks rather than investment quotations for Pakistan. At genuinely industrial scale, the numbers become much larger. A European engineering study for a 21,000-tonne-per-year hydrometallurgical recycling hub estimated capital expenditure of about $320m, while an integrated operation combining mechanical pre-processing and refining was estimated at approximately $440m. These differences explain why asking for the “minimum capital” required for battery recycling can be misleading. A better question is: which part of the recycling chain offers the most practical entry point? For Pakistan, beginning at the lower and middle parts of the chain may offer a more realistic route. Collection networks, battery diagnostics, second-life assessment, dismantling and eventually black-mass production can build commercial experience before firms move towards sophisticated metal recovery. Capital alone, however, does not determine viability. A recycling plant needs sufficient batteries flowing through it. Research consistently shows that recycling economics depend heavily on throughput, battery chemistry, collection and transportation costs, energy and material prices, and the value of recovered metals. Economies of scale can significantly improve commercial feasibility. Chemistry matters as well. Batteries rich in nickel and cobalt can produce more valuable recovered materials, while lithium iron phosphate batteries contain fewer high-value metals. A plant designed around assumptions about today’s battery waste may therefore face different economics as Pakistan’s battery mix changes. This is why the first investment before building a large recycling facility should arguably be information. Pakistan needs reliable estimates of how many lithium-ion batteries are already entering the market, their chemistries, where they are being deployed and when they are expected to reach end of life. Without a predictable feedstock pipeline, even technically sophisticated facilities can struggle commercially. For Pakistani entrepreneurs, therefore, battery recycling need not begin with a multimillion-dollar refinery. It can begin with organised collection, diagnostics and safe dismantling, followed by mechanical processing as volumes increase and eventually chemical recovery when sufficient feedstock and technical capabilities exist. The capital requirement grows at every stage, but so does the potential value captured. The lesson for investors is simple: do not begin by asking how much a battery recycling plant costs. Begin by deciding which part of the battery recycling business you want to build. The writer is a research associate at the Centre of Excellence-CPEC under Pide and the Ministry of Planning and Special Initiatives. Google Maps renames Lake Ontario ‘Lake America’ in US — but not Canada. WASHINGTON: Google redesignated Lake Ontario as “Lake America” on maps seen by US users on Sunday after President Donald Trump announced he was renaming the body of water, with a Canadian official slamming the cross-border tensions as “absolutely backwards.” People in Canada will still see Lake Ontario, the Indigenous-rooted name used for the lake since the 17th century, on their devices and computers, the US-based tech giant said. The shock nomenclatural spat erupted as the latest element of Trump’s “America First” narrative, with longtime allies the United States and Canada ramping up a trade war that has seen Washington and Ottawa slap tit-for-tat tariffs on each other. Apple’s Maps app that comes installed on all iPhones makes no mention of “Lake America” on its maps as of Sunday morning. Google said it made its change in line with the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the official federal database for geographic names. “Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the US, people using Maps in the US will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names,” Google said on its blog. The change mirrors Trump’s unilateral altering of the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America in January 2025 — a move Mexico has also rejected. Ontario is the smallest by surface area of the five Great Lakes, which straddle the Canada-US border between Ontario province and the US state of New York. The province’s premier, Doug Ford, offered fresh criticism Sunday of the trade dispute and Trump’s lake name change. “It’s absolutely backwards. It was like something out of (US comedy TV show) ‘Saturday Night Live’ when he signed a document saying — changed to ‘Lake America.’ No one’s going to call it Lake of America,” Ford told ABC talk show “This Week.” “It’s just so disappointing.” Ford also warned that while a trade war would harm both countries, “it’d be definitely devastating on the US” given that Canada has been by far the largest purchaser of US vehicles. Should those buys dry up, US auto factories would be hit hard. “A tariff on Canada is nothing more than a tax on American people,” he said. “It’s probably the worst move you could ever do.” Canada and the US have a deeply interconnected auto manufacturing sector, and a sizeable portion of parts for US vehicles are made in Canada. Trump himself waded in Sunday to say Americans “want to make our own cars.” “Canada has been ripping us off for years — NO LONGER!” Trump posted on his Truth Social platform. PM Shehbaz to embark on three-day visit to Kyrgyzstan today for SCO summit. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will undertake a three-day official visit to the Kyrgyz Republic from Aug 31 to Sept 2 at the invitation of President Sadyr Nurgozhoevich Zhaparov to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Council of Heads of State meeting, the Foreign Office (FO) said in a statement. “The visit will include participation in the SCO Council of Heads of State meeting, as well as bilateral engagements in the Kyrgyz Republic,” the FO said. It said the premier will be accompanied by Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar, Minister of Commerce Jam Kamal Khan, Minister of Communications Abdul Aleem Khan, Minister of Information and Broadcasting Attaullah Tarar and other senior officials. “During his stay in Bishkek, the prime minister will participate in the meeting of the SCO Council of Heads of State and the SCO Plus Summit,” the statement said. “The prime minister will also assume Pakistan’s chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for 2026-2027,” it said, adding that he would also hold bilateral meetings with the leaders of the participating countries on the sidelines. PM Shehbaz will also participate in the opening ceremony of the World Nomad Games on Aug 31, the statement said. It added that on Sept 2, the prime minister would hold bilateral discussions with the Kyrgyz president on the “entire spectrum of Pakistan-Kyrgyzstan relations”. “The two sides will comprehensively review Pakistan-Kyrgyzstan relations and discuss ways to further deepen bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade and investment, energy, regional connectivity, education, tourism, and people-to-people exchanges,” it said. “The leaders will also exchange views on regional and international developments of mutual interest and cooperation at regional and multilateral fora,” it added. “Pakistan and Kyrgyzstan enjoy warm and fraternal relations, rooted in shared history, faith and cultural affinity, as well as common aspirations for peace, connectivity and prosperity in Central and South Asia,” the FO said. “The forthcoming visit will provide an important opportunity to consolidate the momentum generated by recent high-level exchanges, translate political goodwill into enhanced practical cooperation, and further strengthen the enduring partnership between Pakistan and the Kyrgyz Republic,” the statement concluded. Around a dozen world leaders will head to Bishkek to mark 25 years of the SCO, which comprises 10 member states: India, Iran, China, Pakistan, Russia, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. The two observer states are Afghanistan and Mongolia. Pakistan is set to assume the chairmanship of the SCO’s Council of Heads of State, while next year’s CHS summit will also be hosted by Islamabad.

2 terrorists killed during intelligence-based operation in Balochistan’s Washuk: state media. Two terrorists were killed during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Balochistan’s Washuk district, state-run PTV reported on Monday, citing security sources. In a post on the social media platform X, the state broadcaster said the IBO was conducted in the Palantak area of Washuk as part of the ongoing Operation Radul Fitna against Fitna al Hindustan . The state has designated Balochistan-based terrorist groups as Fitna al Hindustan to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. PTV said the terrorists killed were involved in attacks on the Mashkhel police station and the Customs House. “The terrorists’ vehicle was destroyed during the operation, while a large quantity of weapons and ammunition was also recovered,” it said. High-rises sealed, 3 Islamabad hospitals fined over fire safety violations. ISLAMABAD: Following the recent tragic incident at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), where 14 newborn babies died in a fire, the Capital Development Authority (CDA) has intensified enforcement of fire and life safety regulations across Islamabad, sealing several high-rise buildings and partially sealing two hotels in Blue Area while imposing fines on three hospitals. The CDA imposed a fine of Rs500,000 each on Pims, Polyclinic and its own Capital Hospital for “non-compliance with Fire and Life Safety Requirements”. As part of the enforcement operation in Blue Area, the CDA sealed Shaheed-i-Millat Building, State Life Building, Trade Development Authority of Pakistan Building and Beverly Centre. Teams were also inspecting the National Insurance Company Limited building until the filing of this report. Action follows Pims fire that killed 14 newborns as civic agency intensifies inspections, enforcement Two hotels in Blue Area were partially sealed, with further intake of guests stopped. “Yes, today we have sealed several high-rise buildings in Blue Area, besides partially sealing two hotels. Fines of Rs500,000 each were also imposed on Pims, Polyclinic and CDA’s own hospital,” a CDA official said. An official pastes a ‘sealed’ notice on the State Life Building in Islamabad on Sunday. — White Star The official added that teams had moved towards F-11 to seal an apartment building owned by a politician. “We have reached F-11 and after a while, high-rise apartment buildings owned by a politician will be sealed for non-compliance with rules, despite issuance of several notices,” he said. In a press release, the CDA said it had intensified enforcement of fire and life safety standards across Islamabad, making it clear that the protection of human lives would remain its “topmost priority”. The civic agency said it had sealed Shaheed-i-Millat Secretariat, State Life Building and Trade Development Authority of Pakistan Building in Blue Area following non-compliance with fire safety observations issued earlier by the CDA’s Fire & Emergency Services Directorate. “Chairman CDA Sohail Ashraf has directed the concerned formations of CDA to adopt a zero-tolerance approach towards serious fire safety violations and ensure strict compliance with safety standards,” the press release said. It added that the chairman had emphasised that no building, institution or organisation could be permitted to compromise people’s lives and safety by ignoring essential fire prevention and emergency response requirements. According to the CDA, its Fire & Emergency Services Directorate had been conducting inspections of buildings to identify deficiencies relating to fire prevention, emergency exits, firefighting arrangements, evacuation preparedness and other essential life safety measures. The Building Control Section of the CDA had been advised to rectify identified deficiencies within the prescribed timeframe, the press release said. The CDA chairman also directed relevant departments to maintain close monitoring of fire safety compliance and ensure that safety observations were followed by effective corrective measures. The chairman said fire safety was a collective responsibility, adding that timely installation and maintenance of firefighting equipment, clear emergency exits, proper evacuation arrangements and compliance with safety protocols could save lives during an emergency. “Protection of human lives is the first and foremost responsibility. No compromise will be made on fire and life safety,” the CDA statement said. Meanwhile, the Islamabad High Court was approached against the alleged non-implementation of fire safety laws. A citizen, Malik Naveed Ashiq Awan, through his counsel Advocate Afrasiab Ahmed Rana, filed a petition before the IHC, making the federation, CDA chairman, chief commissioner, Metropolitan Corporation Islamabad (MCI), Higher Education Commission (HEC), Private Educational Regulatory Authority (Pera), Federal Directorate of Education (FDE) and Islamabad Food Authority, among others, respondents. The petitioner contended that 14 newborn babies were burnt alive in a fire at Pims on August 26, raising serious questions about fire safety arrangements at one of the capital’s largest public hospitals. The petition stated that Pims itself allegedly did not have a fire safety no-objection certificate (NOC) from the relevant fire department. Iran targets US military in Jordan, UAE after American attack on Larak Island in latest flare-up. Iran said on Monday it attacked US military targets in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in retaliation for the first American strikes on its territory in a month, marking a fresh flare-up in the six-month war. Tehran’s Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said they struck two US military air bases with ballistic missiles in Washington-allied Jordan, causing “heavy damage”. Jordan’s army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin. The strikes came after the United States said on Sunday it had attacked Iranian rocket launchers on a small island in the Strait of Hormuz. Washington said its attacks were aimed at preventing Iran from launching more sea mines into the strait, days after it announced it had completed clearing explosives from the strategic waterway. “US forces took limited, precise action against IRGC mine laying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz,” the US Central Command (Centcom) wrote on X. The Guards said the US strikes resulted in “casualties” and that their subsequent attack on Jordan was “in response to the US-Zionist aerial aggression”. In a separate statement, IRGC said it attacked the United Arab Emirates’ Al Minhad Air Base with drones, Iranian state TV reported. It said the attack, prompted by the attack on Larak Island, targeted locations where US forces and helicopters were stationed at the base. Meanwhile, Iran’s foreign ministry said armed forces struck US military bases in Jordan in response to the attack on Larak Island. The ministry said the US bases in Jordan had been used to launch and support the attack on Larak. Condemning the attack, the foreign ministry said strikes by Iranian forces on bases in Jordan were “legitimate defence”. Iran “strongly condemned the American military aggression on Larak”, and Iranian forces responded “in accordance with the inherent right of legitimate defence”, it said. The ministry warned that Iran would respond decisively to further military aggression and that the US and parties supporting its actions bore full responsibility for any escalation. The exchange of fire came shortly after the US-Iran war hit the six-month mark, and at a time when hostilities had been subsiding. In recent weeks, the administration of US President Donald Trump has prioritised “economic warfare” over military strikes on Iran. Tehran has effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic sea lane through which one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the United States and Israel triggered hostilities with strikes on Iran on February 28. Bessent signals more sanctions The return to hostilities follows weeks in which the Trump administration has stepped up efforts to punish Tehran and its business partners with costly economic sanctions, shifting away from military options. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters on Sunday new secondary sanctions were likely to be unveiled weekly in the effort to pressure Iran, with an initial focus on banks. “We’re starting with the banks, and we’re telling the banks it’s not okay to have Iranian money and to aid the regime,” Bessent said in an interview. After imposing penalties on the United Arab Emirates branches of Egypt’s Banque Misr on Friday over alleged financial links to Iran, Bessent said the next step may be cutting off an institution entirely from the dollar-based financial system. “You’re going to see a lot more of these every week,” Bessent told Reuters , ahead of a meeting of Group of 20 finance leaders. Unpopular war Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar , have tried for months to bring an end to the war. While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming, and Washington has since declared “economic warfare” against Tehran. A US naval counterblockade of Iranian ports is squeezing petrol supplies in Iran during a shortfall in domestic production, as the US ramps up the pressure. The April ceasefire put an end to the most intense fighting, but sporadic attacks, mainly around the Strait of Hormuz, have dimmed the prospects of a final peace agreement. The last US strike on Iran prior to Sunday’s came on July 29 in response to “an attempted surprise attack on US forces” in the region, the US military said. Earlier in July, Centcom attacked Iran for 13 consecutive nights . Throughout the war, Iran has fought back by striking US facilities and allies in the Gulf region, hitting targets in Kuwait, Oman, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, among others. Its closure of the Strait of Hormuz has caused pain around the world in the form of price hikes and shortages of fertiliser and energy. Oil prices rose after news of the US strikes on Iran. A barrel of North Sea Brent crude, the international benchmark, climbed back above the symbolic $90 threshold. West Texas Intermediate rose to more than $85. The Iran war is deeply unpopular with the US public, with midterm elections looming in November that could overturn Republican control of Congress. In a statement on Friday, US Senator Jack Reed criticised Trump over the war. “Six months later, not a single objective has been achieved,” said Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee. “Indeed, he has weakened our position in the Middle East and the world significantly.”

England captain Joe Root shrugs off concerns over lbw run after Pakistan Test series win. England captain Joe Root is confident of working his way through a dip in form that has seen him trapped lbw nine times in his last 12 innings, and says his record of more than 14,000 Test runs proves he knows how to navigate difficult spells. England’s leading Test run-scorer with 14,208 runs, second only to India’s Sachin Tendulkar (15,921) on the all-time list, has passed 50 only twice during the home summer. “I’ve played this game a long time and I’ve always found ways of solving those problems and working it through,” the 35-year-old told BBC on Sunday. “I don’t see this as being any different. There’s a reason why I’ve got 14,000 runs and a reason why I’ve played the best part of 15 years at this level.” Root’s comments came after England secured a home Test series win over Pakistan at Lord’s where he managed scores of four and 24 before being out lbw in both innings. The build-up to the second Test was overshadowed by the controversy surrounding fast bowler Brydon Carse, who was dropped from the squad following an incident outside a nightclub in Derby. Root said he had addressed the issue with his players and stressed the need for the squad to celebrate successes responsibly. “It’s hard to win Test matches, it’s hard to win Test series. Enjoy it and celebrate it, but in a sensible and grown-up way,” he said.

Modi’s hate policy. ORGANISED hate against the marginalised has defined Indian politics under Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination has urged India to address hate speech, discrimination and hate crimes, advising respect for rights and refraining from expelling Rohingya, Bengali-speaking Muslims and migrants. Racially motivated violence, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detentions, torture and sexual abuse have also been highlighted. While law and order is the state’s duty, India Hate Lab data in 2025 showed that oppression thrived in BJP-ruled parts and fell in opposition-governed states. The pattern is set. Political leaders create the mood, the media broadcasts it, and BJP-linked elements get to work on the ground. The police look on. Mr Modi’s political toolkit relies on incendiary rhetoric and divisive agendas that avert attention from government failures. This strategy has sustained his political career — the 2002 Gujarat pogrom marked his rise. But it is destroying India’s social fabric and disregarding the constitutional guarantee of impartiality. As global scrutiny mounts, India’s democratic credentials stand weakened. What stands out in the UN’s observations is how the government has exploited the caste matrix that divides Hindus “by function and social standing” with unspeakable cruelty. Rabid intolerance for inclusive and progressive values cannot surge without rulers granting impunity to offenders. That is how othering ensures silence and fear. Mr Modi’s regime has deepened social divisions, turned the Muslim identity into a slur and supervised a dramatic shift in the sociopolitical setting whereby historical truths have been erased from textbooks, and customs, including religious festivals, are being reframed to suit the BJP’s pitch of Hindutva supremacy. However, after the Cockroach Janta Party-led protests , opposition parties are taking a far more aggressive position against the oppression of both minorities and lower castes. Dictators are remembered by the bloodstains they leave behind. Published in Dawn, August 31st, 2026

Nepal teams seek hundreds trapped in hydropower tunnels after deadly floods. Nepal’s rescue teams, helped by Chinese and Indian experts, worked overnight to reach hundreds of people believed to be stuck inside blocked hydropower project tunnels in the aftermath of last week’s Himalayan flood that carved a trail of destruction in the country’s valley towns and villages as well as across the border in China. The unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris on the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday, blamed on a glacier collapse, killed more than 900 people and nearly 5,000 are still missing. Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, have been buried in shallow graves as they began decomposing in the humid weather in the plains of the Himalayan country after being swept down the mountains by the torrent. Nepali officials said that the focus was on reaching the hundreds of workers believed to be trapped inside about half a dozen hydropower project tunnels that had been blocked by mud and rock debris. Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night as workers watched. Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel. A rescuer works at the entrance of a tunnel at Chilime Hydropower Plant as rescue operations continue for people trapped inside following deadly flash floods and a mudslide, in Rasuwa, Nepal on August 29, 2026. —AFP Nepal’s disaster management authority said that 933 people were missing from hydropower projects in the flood-hit region. The Red Cross has estimated that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster, which China has linked to the effects of climate change. On Monday, Nepali authorities said 903 people had died, with 4,247 missing, including the 933 at hydropower projects. On the Chinese side, authorities said 16 people were killed in Gyirong County and 546 were missing. Complete assessment of damage challenging, Nepal PM says “A large amount of debris has been deposited, and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Reuters . Our main focus is on opening the tunnels. Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the flood was an unprecedented and devastating natural disaster and it remained challenging to compile a complete assessment of the damage. Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens, he said in a Facebook post late on Sunday, adding that nearly 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations, besides civilian workers and volunteers. Chinese President Xi Jinping, on a visit to Kyrgyzstan, said Beijing is making every effort to search for missing people following the disaster, Xinhua reported on Monday. Beijing has said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were unaccounted for in Tibet, near a key border crossing with Nepal. China’s state-run CCTV reported Beijing has mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least 220 million yuan to support relief efforts and has been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing. Risk from lakes and landslides Although Nepal has said that it does not need foreign help in general rescue and search, it has leaned on giant neighbours India and China for their expertise in tunnel rescue. Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s rivers. China’s state television CCTV said that another lake formed upstream by a landslide had largely drained as water flowed out naturally. The landslide occurred 2.8 km downstream from the first lake formed by debris of the glacier collapse. Authorities are now monitoring an impact crater carved out near the site of the glacier collapse on the Nepalese side, which had expanded to 174,000 square metres by Saturday evening, state media said. Ayush Khadka’s mother Monac Khadka mourns during her son’s cremation in the aftermath of flash floods, in Nepal’s Chitwan district on August 31, 2026. —AFP The crater had an estimated reservoir of 2.5 million cubic metres, which if breached, could lead to a chain reaction to lakes further downstream, authorities warned. CCTV said there is risk of further landslides along the river that could create additional lakes, as investigators identified eight high-risk locations for geological disasters. The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, the state broadcaster reported, saying it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters” on the Tibetan plateau. Two Nepali officials told Reuters that China had not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels following a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that a lack of data sharing could hamper future disaster preparedness. China’s foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment on the meeting.

Imran's hospital transfer: SC turns down Uzma's application seeking early hearing of contempt plea. ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court on Monday turned down yet another request by Dr Uzma Khan, the sister of incarcerated PTI founder Imran Khan, for swift contempt of court proceedings against government functionaries for violating the August 18 order direction Imran’s transfer to a private hospital. The contempt of court petition has already been fixed before a three-judge SC bench, consisting of Justice Shahid Waheed, Justice Naeem Akhtar Afghan and Justice Ishtiaq Ibrahim, for September 16. The same bench will resume hearing pending cases concerning the ex-premier’s health and family meetings on September 16. The bench had last heard the pleas on Aug 18 and ordered Imran’s transfer to Shifa International Hospital within two days. Ignoring Uzma’s request for an early hearing, the SC office on Monday repeated its justification that the fixation policy required proceedings to be conducted turn-wise. It said that already 94 different criminal original petitions belonging to the same category were pending before the SC for hearing. It said that the fixation policy required that cases be fixed for hearing when it was their turn. Last week, the SC’s registrar office had turned down Uzma’s first request for early hearing of the contempt petition. In her second application, filed through Advocate Uzair Karamat Bhandari on August 27, she had stated that the contempt of court petition against the government functionaries for violating court directions on Imran’s transfer to a private hospital was meant to ensure immediate implementation of the Aug 18 order. The early hearing will serve the interest of justice, protection of life and health and due enforcement of the SC’s Aug 18 orders, the application had contended. It added that the subject matter of the petition concerned the life, health, dignity and physical well-being of Imran, who was a “national hero” and a former prime minister, whose health was deteriorating and whose life was stated to be in jeopardy, the application feared. The application had pleaded for the reconsideration of the decision to fix the hearing for Sept 16. It further stated that the reasons set out regarding the fixation policy could not justify such a long delay in the hearing. The applicant had pleaded that there was nothing in the case which the SC’s fixation policy prevented immediate hearing of the contempt petition. In fact, the fixation policy clearly prioritises liberty-related matters, especially where they arise due to non-compliance with court orders, it said. Uzma’s applications came in response to the events which unfolded following SC’s order. Despite the court’s Aug 18 order stipulating Imran’s transfer to the hospital within two days, the government took the PTI founder to Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), a government hospital, for a check-up and then subsequently transported him back to prison. At the time, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar had blamed “the security situation created by PTI workers on the way to and outside” the hospital for the diversion. The PTI has denied the allegations and accused the government of deliberately flouting the court’s orders.

Bangladesh, India 'very sincere' over delayed cricket series: BCB president. Bangladesh and India are “sincere” in their search for a new date for a white-ball series that was first supposed to take place last year, Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) President Tamim Iqbal said. The three one-day internationals (ODIs) and three T20 matches in Bangladesh were originally planned for August 2025, but then political relations soured between the two countries. The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) then said the series would be played this September, but there is no sign of it happening imminently. “Both boards are very sincere that this thing happens,” Tamim said on the podcast Not out Noman on Sunday. “Both BCCI and BCB, we are looking at windows as well, which time what can be done.” He added, “Intentions are very positive.” There was no immediate response from the BCCI. Dhaka and New Delhi have been at odds since a 2024 mass uprising toppled then-Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina. She fled to India, her long-time ally, where she remains in hiding . In February, Bangladesh refused to send a team to India for the T20 World Cup, citing security concerns. India last toured Bangladesh for a cricket series in 2022. Bangladesh visited India in September-October 2024.

IHC seeks replies from ministries, Pemra, PTA on plea seeking to regulate children's social media use. ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Monday sought responses from relevant ministries and authorities on a petition seeking a framework to regulate social media use by children under 16 years of age. The plea, filed by petitioner Waqas Nasir through advocates Muhammad Jalal Haider and Yahya Farid Khawaja earlier this month, seeks legislation on the matter and the introduction of an effective age-verification mechanism for social media accounts. It was taken up by IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfaraz Dogar, who issued notices to the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Ministry of Interior, Ministry of Law and Justice, Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) and Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (Pemra) and directed them to submit their replies within 15 days. During the hearing, Advocates Haider and Khawaja appeared before the court. Advocate Haider argued that an effective age-verification mechanism should be introduced for social media accounts operated by children. He contended that legislation was urgently required to protect children from cyberbullying, online harassment, harmful and inappropriate content and other risks associated with the use of social media platforms. The lawyer argued that safeguarding the best interests of children was a “constitutional and legal responsibility of the state” and that the government should introduce effective legislation in line with international practices. When Justice Dogar enquired whether Pemra had any law dealing with the issue, Advocate Haider said Pemra had legal powers to take action against a person on the basis of a complaint, but currently, there was no specific legislation regulating children’s access to social media. The IHC CJ further asked whether any law had so far been enacted specifically for this purpose, to which the lawyer replied in the negative. Subsequently, Justice Dogar issued notices to the relevant ministries and authorities, seeking their responses within 15 days. The court also directed the law officer to ensure implementation of the notices. The plea In his petition, Nasir urged the court to direct the government to formulate a comprehensive legal and regulatory framework for the online protection of children, including special safeguards governing their access to social media. The plea contended that children were increasingly exposed to the harmful effects of social media, including cyberbullying, online harassment, and inappropriate or harmful content, requiring the state to introduce a comprehensive legal and regulatory mechanism for their protection. The petitioner urged the court to direct the government to formulate a policy covering digital rights, privacy, and mental and physical safety of children, and to impose specific responsibilities on social media platforms to safeguard minors online. The plea stated that several countries around the world had already introduced age restrictions and safety measures for children’s use of social media and contended that legislation in this connection would be part of an emerging international trend for protecting children in the digital environment. It relied on the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child and General Comment No. 25, arguing that protecting the best interests of children was not merely a policy objective but a legal obligation of the state. The matter had also come into the limelight in the Punjab Assembly last month, when a resolution was submitted for a nationwide ban on social media accounts for children under the age of 16 without parental consent. The resolution, moved by MPA Sarah Ahmad, urged the provincial government to recommend to the federal government to introduce comprehensive legislation to regulate children’s access to social media platforms and strengthen online safety measures.

IHC chief justice seeks copy of inquiry report on fire at Pims, details of action taken. ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) has sought the report submitted to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on the fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) and details of the action taken, while also questioning the culpability of the hospital’s executive director (ED). Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfaraz Dogar passed the directions while hearing two separate petitions related to the Pims tragedy. During the hearing of a petition filed by lawyer Qasim Iqbal Jalali seeking a judicial inquiry into the incident, Additional Attorney General (AAG) Rashid Hafeez, Deputy Attorney General Faisal Irfan and Assistant Attorney General Azmat Bashir Tarar appeared before the court. Justice Dogar termed the Pims fire a “terrible incident” and observed that the loss of 14 children was extremely serious. The petitioner’s counsel argued that the government had constituted committees comprising bureaucrats, questioning how the officials of one department could conduct an inquiry into their own colleagues. “How can bureaucrats inquire into their own department?” the counsel asked. The chief justice questioned the legal basis of the request for a judicial inquiry, asking the lawyer under which law the court could order such an inquiry and where the Inquiry Act empowered the IHC to issue such directives. The counsel referred to the commission constituted after the Punjab Institute of Cardiology incident . The chief justice observed that the said commission had not been constituted by the court, adding that such matters fell within the government’s domain. “If there is any matter with us, I will ask one of my judges to look into it,” Justice Dogar remarked. The counsel maintained that “no one can be the judge of his own actions” and argued that responsibility had not been fixed in the inquiry report submitted so far. AAG Hafeez informed the court that the health secretary had been suspended on the day of the incident, while hospital officials had subsequently been suspended on the basis of an interim inquiry report. Justice Dogar again termed the incident extremely tragic and asked whether any action was still being taken and whether there was any restriction preventing the court from passing an order. The court sought the report submitted to the prime minister, along with details of the action taken so far and directed the federation to submit a detailed response. A separate petition also sought removal of the Pims ED from office — who has already been suspended — and action over the tragedy. The petitioner’s counsel highlighted the conditions at the hospital and questioned the utilisation of its massive budget. The counsel told the court that the deaths of the children were horrific and requested that the Pims ED be removed from his post. “How can the court give a direction to remove him from the post?” Chief Justice Dogar asked. The counsel contended that Pims has an annual budget of around Rs20 to Rs22 billion, yet several children were being accommodated on a single bed. He questioned where the budget was being spent and urged the court to order the executive director’s removal and return his services to his parent department. The chief justice observed that he believed the Pims ED had already been removed from the post, referring to the prime minister’s orders to suspend Prof Dr Imran Sikandar and seven others. National Institutes of Health (NIH) Chief Executive Officer Dr Mohammad Salman has taken charge of the post after being appointed as the acting Pims ED. The counsel replied that although the ED had been removed, no responsibility had been fixed against him and he had not been held responsible in the inquiry report either. AAG Hafeez told the court that the report currently available was only an interim report and that the complete inquiry report would be submitted within five days. The chief justice specifically asked whether responsibility had so far been fixed against the Pims ED. The court sought a report on the matter and adjourned the hearing. CDA response sought over alleged lack of safety NOCs Separately, the IHC has sought a response from the federal capital’s administration over the alleged non-implementation of fire safety laws and regulations in Islamabad. Justice Dogar heard the petition filed by citizen Malik Naveed Ashiq Awan through his counsel, Advocate Afrasiab Ahmed Rana. The petition was filed in the wake of the Pims incident. The petitioner contended that even a major healthcare facility such as Pims did not have the requisite fire department no-objection certificate (NOC). The petition further alleged that commercial, educational and medical buildings across Islamabad were operating without fire safety NOCs and that several buildings lacked essential fire-fighting equipment, emergency exits and fire alarms. The petitioner pleaded that the Islamabad Fire Prevention and Life Safety Regulations 2010 should be implemented in letter and spirit. The petition sought directions for an immediate fire safety audit of all buildings in the federal capital and the sealing of buildings operating without valid fire safety NOCs. It also sought the establishment of a regular inspection mechanism to identify and monitor buildings that are illegal or pose a threat to public safety. The court issued notices to the home secretary, Metropolitan Corporation Islamabad (MCI), and the offices of the Capital Development Authority (CDA) chairman and Islamabad chief commissioner — both roles served by retired Lt Sohail Ashraf — seeking their responses. The petition maintained that the Pims fire had exposed serious shortcomings in the enforcement of fire safety regulations and called for immediate institutional action to prevent similar incidents in the future. Following the Pims incident, CDA intensified enforcement of fire and life safety regulations across Islamabad, sealing several high-rise buildings and partially sealing two hotels in Blue Area. It also imposed a fine of Rs500,000 each on Pims, Polyclinic and its own Capital Hospital for “non-compliance with Fire and Life Safety Requirements”. Final inquiry report awaited Meanwhile, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said that the inquiry committee’s investigation into the Pims incident had not been completed yet. Speaking to the media in Islamabad, he said the inquiry was ongoing, not just into the gynaecology department but into all departments of the hospital. “More names can come up in the final report. Anyone found guilty of negligence will be punished,” Chaudhry said. Acknowledging that “the innocent lives lost cannot be brought back”, the minister stressed that action against those responsible was essential to avoid similar incidents in the future. Speaking on behalf of PM Shehbaz, Chaudhry vowed that zero tolerance would be shown towards those found guilty of negligence. Safety arrangements and precautions at Pims were being closely monitored by the health ministry, he told the media.
