Pakistani climber Asma Mushtaq's body recovered on GB's Spantik Peak nearly 10 days after her death. GILGIT: A ground team recovered the body of deceased Pakistani climber Asma Mushtaq from Gilgit-Baltistan’s Spantik Peak on Monday, almost 10 days after her death on the 7,027-metre-tall mountain. The 34-year-old climber died on Aug 20 while descending from the mountain after suffering from high-altitude sickness. Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) Secretary General Ayaz Shigri told Dawn that a five-member team, comprising high-altitude mountaineers from Shigar, had initiated a new recovery mission on Friday after earlier attempts remained unsuccessful due to heavy snowfall. Earlier recovery missions were carried out by a six-member team, and the new team comprised Mehboob, Hussain Ali, Mazahir Hussain, Mehboob Ali, Muhammad Abidin and Abbas Ali, who led the operation, Shigri said. These volunteers were from Arundu in Shigar and carried out the operation as a self-funded mission, he added. The rescue team began the operation at 3am today and found the body after around eight hours of searching, at around 11am. The team recovered the body near Camp 3 of the peak, which is located at a height of approximately 6,250 metres, Shigri said. He added that the body would be brought back to Camp 2 today and Pakistan Army helicopters were expected to airlift Mushtaq’s body to Skardu after its arrival at the base camp later. Shigri had told Dawn the day that Mushtaq died that she was part of a five-member Pakistani women’s expedition team that summited Spantik, which included climbers Zoni Aslam, Zaba Shigri, Shama and Sohana. The mountaineer had successfully reached the 7,027m summit of Spantik and was in good health at the time, the ACP said in statements issued on Thursday. However, she developed a serious high-altitude medical emergency at an elevation of about 6,400m during her descent. High-altitude sickness encompasses a range of pulmonary and cerebral conditions caused by hypoxia, or oxygen deprivation, due to rapid ascent and inadequate acclimatisation to high altitudes. Climate change-induced shifts in weather patterns have worsened conditions on the peaks of the Karakoram Range in GB, creating serious difficulties for mountaineers. Experts have also pointed out that bringing a body down from a high-altitude peak, particularly from above 6,000m, is an extremely risky and challenging task. In many cases, bodies at such extreme altitudes are left and buried under the snow rather than being brought down. Sajid Sadpara buried the body of his father, renowned Pakistani mountaineer Ali Sadpara, at around 8,000m on K2 in 2021.

Hague court orders India to uphold Indus Waters Treaty, suspend work on its hydropower project. The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) on Monday ordered India to uphold the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) with Pakistan and suspend work on a hydro project in occupied Kashmir. Water and the IWT remain a contentious issue between India and Pakistan, following New Delhi’s unilateral abeyance of the accord in April last year — a move that was followed by a brief military conflict between the two sides in May 2025. Following India’s move, Pakistan termed any attempt to suspend its water share an “act of war”, noting the IWT had no provision for unilateral suspension. It later argued that Delhi’s action was a violation of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. In its order, the PCA backed Pakistan’s stance, declaring that the IWT between the two countries remained fully in force, as India had no justification for ending or suspending the agreement. The Hague-based court issued an award on the status of the IWT “in respect of India’s decision on abeyance” and an order on Pakistan’s application dated March 4 regarding “interim measures” concerning the Ratle hydro-electric plant. In a press release detailing its ruling, the PCA said it “examined the potential grounds upon which India could suspend or terminate the treaty, including the grounds cited by India in its public statements”. “In a unanimous decision, the court found that none of these grounds could justify suspension or termination of the treaty.” It declared that the IWT “remains fully in force, and India must observe its obligations under the treaty, including those relating to the design and operation of its hydro-electric projects on the Western Rivers”. The IWT allocates the eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — to India, while the western rivers — Indus, Jhelum and Chenab — are largely allocated to Pakistan. The 1960 water-sharing agreement has also established mechanisms for data-sharing and dispute resolution. During the proceedings, Pakistan requested the court to address the “design of certain components of the run-of-river hydro-electric projects that India is permitted by the IWT to construct on the Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab rivers and their tributaries (“western rivers”), before those rivers flow into Pakistan”, the PCA statement said. The proceedings in the interim measures’ application concerned India’s Kishenganga Hydro-Electric Plant (KHEP) and the Ratle Hydro-Electric Plant (RHEP). The court noted that the Kishenganga and Ratle plants were “also the subject of proceedings” before a World Bank-appointed neutral expert, who is expected to issue a final decision in July 2027 on whether they were in line with the IWT. In its order, the PCA unanimously decided to “impose measures prohibiting India from concreting the RHEP dam wall and power intake structure above certain levels until 90 days after the neutral expert’s final decision”. The court also imposed a reporting measure relating to the RHEP Construction Schedule until shortly after the neutral expert’s final decision. It declined to grant two other measures requested by Pakistan. The PCA noted that the IWT “does not provide for one party to terminate or suspend the operation of the treaty, or for ‘abeyance’”. The IWT provides that it will remain in force unless modified or terminated by India and Pakistan acting together through adoption of a further treaty. The court examined possible grounds for India’s action outside the treaty — ie under customary international law rules — but found that “there is no rule allowing a state to unilaterally terminate or suspend the operation of a treaty based on its ‘sovereignty’”, as argued by India. The order identified three of the “few, highly restricted grounds” upon which a state could unilaterally terminate or suspend the operation of a treaty: material breach of the pact by a party, fundamental change of circumstances, and effect of armed conflict. In examining these possible scenarios, the court considered India’s claim that Pakistan had violated the IWT’s “cooperative spirit” of the IWT by failing to enter into negotiations to modify the treaty. The Court of Arbitration was chaired by Professor Sean D. Murphy of the United States. The other members were Professor Wouter Buytaert of Belgium, Professor Jeffrey P. Minear of the United States, Judge Awn Shawkat Al-Khasawneh of Jordan, and Dr Donald Blackmore of Australia. Proceedings Pakistan had initiated the arbitration proceedings regarding the western rivers in August 2016, the PCA press release recalled. However, in December that year, the World Bank decided to “ pause ” the process of appointing the chairman of the Court of Arbitration and the neutral expert. This pause was lifted in 2022, following which a neutral expert was appointed. After India unilaterally held the IWT in abeyance in April 2025, the PCA considered its effect on the court’s competence in a “Supplemental Award on Competence” issued on June 27 that year. The court held that “India’s decision on the ‘abeyance’ of the treaty cannot limit the competence of the Court over this dispute”. “However, the court did not go further in determining whether the Indus Waters Treaty remained in force,” it added. On March 4, Pakistan filed an application before the court to “determine the present status of the Treaty in light of India’s decision on ‘abeyance’”. The PCA noted that India was invited to indicate whether it would participate in the proceedings but received “no response”. The court then directed Pakistan to “file a written memorial further detailing its application and held a hearing at the Peace Palace in The Hague” from April 26 to 28. While India did not participate by making written or oral submissions in response to Pakistan’s application, the PCA sought to consider India’s positions on the matters “to the extent they could be discerned from India’s statements and conduct outside of these proceedings (including Indian government communications to Pakistan and to the neutral expert, and public statements made by Indian officials)”. More to follow

Mir Raza murder case: SHC reserves order on family's plea seeking JIT. KARACHI: The Sindh High Court (SHC) on Monday reserved its verdict on a plea seeking the formation of a joint investigation team (JIT) in the Mir Raza Ali murder case. Ali, a 25-year-old Karachi-based businessman, was found dead with a gunshot wound in Gulistan-i-Jauhar last month, a day after he was reported missing on July 28. His family, which has raised questions about the case’s investigation and accused authorities of trying to bury the facts, had moved the SHC last week against a decision of the provincial government to form a judicial commission and sought the formation of a JIT instead. However, authorities proceeded with the commission, with Justice Omar Sial appointed as its head. A two-member constitutional bench, headed by Justice Adnan Karim Memon, took up the family’s petition on Monday. The Sindh advocate general (AG), prosecutor general, Karachi police surgeon, police officials, the case’s investigating officer, Ali’s family, and their counsel Jibran Nasir appeared before the court during the hearing. Nasir reiterated the demand for a JIT, following which the court enquired about the difference between a JIT and a judicial commission. To that, the state’s lawyer said, “A JIT will investigate the case from various angles while a commission can provide assistance in the investigation”. Nasir reminded the court that to investigate the Gul Plaza blaze, a JIT and a commission were formed separately. He further alleged that police personnel had destroyed evidence in the case, adding that this was also mentioned in his plea. Nasir also accused police of “spreading false news through the media” and added that no statements were recorded several days after the case was registered and that the “crime scene was set on fire”. “It was set on fire to search for a bullet, just as the crime scene was washed in Rawalpindi,” he said, seemingly referring to the washing of the site of the killing of former prime minister Benazir Bhutto in 2007. He said no action was taken against the police officers “who destroyed the case and tampered with the evidence”. “We had demanded departmental action,” Nasir said, adding that it was the investigation team’s job to find the suspects. The Sindh advocate general informed the court that the “commission’s function was to investigate the negligence (in the investigation)”. Nasir maintained that “the SC has in the past also granted permission to form a JIT as well in case of administrative sabotage”. “There is sabotage at the highest level of the police in this case,” he said, recalling that police had declared the case shut “even before Ali’s grave was dug” — a reference to the exhumation of Ali’s body for a second autopsy after the Karachi police surgeon pointed out loopholes in the first post-mortem report. When the court observed that the government had already formed a commission, Nasir argued that the commission would be supported by the “same team that has failed to trace the suspects even after a month”. For his part, the Sindh AG clarified that the provincial government was “not against the family”. Following these arguments, the court reserved its order on the petition. The case The case has been mired in controversy since the beginning. While Ali’s family was convinced that he was kidnapped, tortured and murdered, police had initially built the case around the possibility that he died by suicide. Days after the recovery of Ali’s body, Karachi Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed had told Geo News that the post-mortem findings in the case had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. On August 6, a Karachi court took up an application by Ali’s father, allowed the exhumation of his body, ordered the formation of a medico-legal board for the purpose and directed that a second autopsy of Ali’s body be conducted. The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with police surgeon Dr Sumaiyya Syed as the convener. However, in the early hours of August 7, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed. But Ali’s family rejected the new board, which also resulted in the deferment of the planned exhumation on Friday. Meanwhile, the counsel for Ali’s family, Nasir accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts. The Sindh government then restored the original medical board, following which Ali’s body was exhumed on August 8. A day later, the Sindh inspector general of police’s (IG) office notified the reconstitution of the investigating team probing Ali’s death while Karachi Additional IG Azad Khan transferred the investigation into Ali’s murder to Zaman Town police station from Ferozabad Police Station, where the case was registered. The order for the probe team’s reconstitution also showed that a murder charge had been added to the first information report. The same day, the Sindh government decided to seek a judicial commission for the case’s investigation, only to defer the plan a day later after Ali’s family said they had made no such demand and had faith in the new investigation team. On Aug 19, Ali’s parents, Mir Hussain and Mariam Hussain, wrote to Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah, seeking his “direct supervision of the murder investigation”. They also urged the chief minister to order an investigation and departmental inquiry into the previous investigation team and immediately suspend the officers involved. The provincial government acknowledged the letter and announced the decision on Aug 23 to form a judicial commission to determine whether the investigation in the case was being conducted impartially and to investigate the circumstances surrounding Ali’s death. However, soon after the announcement, the counsel for Ali’s family raised objections and later approached the SHC. The petition was filed on August 24 in objection to the provincial government’s decision to form a judicial commission and sought the formation of an independent and multi-agency JIT “comprising officers who have had no previous involvement in the case” in place of the commission. The commission held the first hearing on Friday, and has summoned medico-legal officer Osama Sheikh, who had performed Ali’s first autopsy. It also issued notices to the deceased’s family, their lawyer and a provincial government focal person.

PM Shehbaz meets Iranian President Pezeshkian on sidelines of SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Kyrgyzstan on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Council of Heads of State meeting on Monday, according to the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO). Pezeshkian welcomed PM Shehbaz in Bishkek for his three-day official visit from Aug 31 to Sep 2 and the two leaders held a meeting, the PMO said on X. Earlier, the prime minister reached the Kyrgyz Republic on a three-day official visit, from Aug 31 to Sept 2, at the invitation of President Sadyr Nurgozhoevich Zhaparov to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Council of Heads of State meeting. Adylbek Kasymaliev, chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers, welcomed PM Shehbaz upon his arrival at Manas International Airport, the government’s official account on social media platform X stated . Announcing the premier’s departure, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said he would address the SCO summit and “present Pakistan’s stance on various regional and global issues”. It added that Minister of Commerce Jam Kamal Khan, Minister of Communications Abdul Aleem Khan, and Minister of Information and Broadcasting Attaullah Tarar were accompanying PM Shehbaz. Earlier in the day, the Foreign Office had issued a statement on PM Shehbaz’s visit, saying that it would include participation in the SCO Council of Heads of State meeting, as well as bilateral engagements in the Kyrgyz Republic. “During his stay in Bishkek, the prime minister will participate in the meeting of the SCO Council of Heads of State and the SCO Plus Summit,” the statement said. “The prime minister will also assume Pakistan’s chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for 2026-2027,” it said, adding that he would also hold bilateral meetings with the leaders of the participating countries on the sidelines. PM Shehbaz will also participate in the opening ceremony of the World Nomad Games on Aug 31, the statement said. It added that on Sept 2, the prime minister would hold bilateral discussions with the Kyrgyz president on the “entire spectrum of Pakistan-Kyrgyzstan relations”. “The two sides will comprehensively review Pakistan-Kyrgyzstan relations and discuss ways to further deepen bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade and investment, energy, regional connectivity, education, tourism, and people-to-people exchanges,” it said. “The leaders will also exchange views on regional and international developments of mutual interest and cooperation at regional and multilateral fora,” it added. “Pakistan and Kyrgyzstan enjoy warm and fraternal relations, rooted in shared history, faith and cultural affinity, as well as common aspirations for peace, connectivity and prosperity in Central and South Asia,” the FO said. “The forthcoming visit will provide an important opportunity to consolidate the momentum generated by recent high-level exchanges, translate political goodwill into enhanced practical cooperation, and further strengthen the enduring partnership between Pakistan and the Kyrgyz Republic,” the statement concluded. Around a dozen world leaders will head to Bishkek to mark 25 years of the SCO, which comprises 10 member states: India, Iran, China, Pakistan, Russia, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. The two observer states are Afghanistan and Mongolia. Pakistan is set to assume the chairmanship of the SCO’s Council of Heads of State, while next year’s CHS summit will also be hosted by Islamabad.

Tripartite agreement to be called ‘Makkah Defence Alliance’, with first secretary general from Pakistan: Turkish FM Fidan. Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Monday said that the tripartite agreement between Ankara, Islamabad and Riyadh will be known as “Makkah Defence Alliance”, with its first secretary general to be from Pakistan. He made the announcement while addressing a press conference following the first meeting under the agreement held in Istanbul. Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, and Defence Minister Khawaja Asif represented Pakistan at the meeting. Foreign and defence ministers of the three countries, as well as top military officials, gathered for a family photo ahead of the meeting in Istanbul’s Ciragan Palace. In his press conference, Fidan said his country hosted the first meeting of the strategic defence and political committee on Monday. He said the meeting was held “in relation to the concrete steps that are going to be taken for the implementation of the agreement” and an exchange of views was held for that purpose. “As of today, we have started the process of establishing the institutional structure of the alliance,” Fidan said, announcing that the agreement’s official name will be “Makkah Defence Alliance”. “There is a secretariat that has been established in Riyadh, and the first secretary general will be appointed amongst our Pakistani brothers,” he said. He said that during the meeting, decisions were taken on “how and when to begin institutionalisation and all our brothers expressed views during the meeting”. Fidan hoped that decisions taken in the meeting will have “excellent results”. “For the future of a secure, stable and prosperous region, this alliance is based on international principles such as respecting the sovereignty of other states, territorial integrity and not intervening in internal affairs,” he said, adding that the alliance was not against any country. He maintained that the alliance was “open for the partnership and participation of any other country”. However, Fidan stressed that while the alliance was open, “there are some conditions, rules and standards”, adding that the alliance’s nature was such that it was “expected to expand”. Stressing the need for institutionalisation of the alliance, he said: “If an ally wants to join, the alliance should be functional in a proper manner by then.” He added that the alliance did not “eliminate our countries’ responsibilities to other agreements or alliances”. Fidan hoped that with Monday’s meeting, the three countries had demonstrated readiness to take responsibility for the security and stability of the region. “We will closely cooperate with friendly countries, and we will continue coordinating our efforts,” he said. Fidan also noted that the lack of “alliances and trust” between regional countries had given rise to security problems. According to Anadolu Agency , Fidan, National Defence Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu represented Turkiye at the meeting earlier in the day. Representing Saudi Arabia, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Chief of General Staff General Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili attended the meeting. Anadolu Agency also shared a video showing the participants seated in a hall, with Fidan seated in the middle. The clip showed Fidan greeting Dar, CDF Munir and others at the venue. In a statement issued on Sunday, the Foreign Office (FO) said the meeting will comprise the Strategic Political and Defence Committee established under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. “Pakistan’s participation in the meeting signifies Pakistan’s historic bonds of friendship with the brotherly countries of Turkiye and Saudi Arabia, as well as its desire for lasting regional peace and stability,” the FO said. The maiden ministerial meeting under the Makkah pact is being seen as the first step towards establishing a framework for trilateral strategic and defence cooperation. According to an AFP report, the participants plan to address boosting defence capabilities, the interoperability of their armed forces, and their cooperation in the defence industry. Meanwhile, TRT reported that the meeting is expected to outline the framework for a secretariat and other relevant mechanisms, as well as establish a roadmap for steps to be taken in the coming period. The joint defence pact signed on August 7 empowers the member states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. Bilateral meetings Ahead of the trilateral pact’s inaugural moot, the signatories held multiple bilateral meetings in Istanbul. CDF Munir met Turkish National Defence Minister Yaşar Güler ahead of the first meeting under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Istanbul. In a post on the social media platform X, the Turkish Ministry of National Defence shared a video of CDF Munir meeting Güler. The Turkish minister also held a separate meeting with Asif, with Chief of General Staff General Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu in attendance. According to Radio Pakistan , Asif and the Turkish leadership agreed to enhance joint defence cooperation in the region. Meanwhile, Turkiye’s foreign minister met his Saudi counterpart on the margins of the trilateral moot. Fidan had already held a meeting with Dar on Sunday. Both the deputy premier and the army chief, had arrived in Turkiye a day earlier.

De Lima seeks all-out protection of mangroves amid heavy rains, floods; warns vs earth-balling. House Senior Deputy Minority Leader and Mamamayang Liberal (ML) Party-list Rep. Leila de Lima is prodding the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to suspend its earth-balling and relocation of mangroves. This, as De Lima expressed concern over the destructive impact of the recent strong typhoons and "Habagat" as well as climate change on the livelihoods and lives of Filipinos. Earth-balling is defined as the practice of digging up a tree with its surrounding soil to form a compact, circular mass, which is then protected during transport to a new location. During the House budget briefing on the proposed 2027 budget of the DENR on Aug. 26, De Lima asked about the status of the DENR Memorandum dated Oct. 8, 2025, which provides interim operational guidance and conditions on the earth-balling and relocation of mangroves in exceptional circumstances. “We understand that there is a technical working group (TWG) that was recently created regarding the earth-balling of mangroves. I am wondering why that memorandum was issued at all, even before consultations, or even before the creation of TWG, or a scientific study. What exactly is the survival rate?” De Lima asked during the briefing. "All of these things should have been confirmed or verified first before allowing the issuance of this memorandum. Yes, it is considered interim operational guidance, but is it really interim, or is it now a de facto policy na mag-allow ng earth-balling of mangroves for flagship infrastructure?” she added. Responding to De Lima, DENR Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna said that, amid numerous requests for permits for earth-balling for government projects, the agency deemed it appropriate at the time, under sustainable development that they are following, to issue interim guidelines through a memorandum specifying certain methods or guidelines to be followed. Cuna also shared that the DENR was in consultation with the Ecosystem Research and Development Bureau (ERDB), the Biodiversity Management Bureau (BMB) and the Forest Management Bureau. According to Cuna, they requested these agencies to come up with a study particularly on the survival rate. “We're encouraged by the initial results that have been sent to us already, but for us to be able to to really extensively complete the study, we are targeting December of this year,” the DENR chief said. De Lima stressed that the DENR must be more forthright about study’s findings, given the extremely low, if not zero, survival rate of mangrove earth-balling. She then urged the DENR to first suspend the implementation, if not do away with the memorandum altogether. Cuna committed to evaluate the matter in light of ongoing developments. Last July 2026, De Lima filed House Resolution (HR) No. 1206 seeking to conduct an inquiry into the DENR memorandum as this directly conflicts with the Philippines’ internationally-endorsed commitments and undermines the country’s credibility and standing as a steward of global mangrove conservation. According to HR No. 1206, the memorandum contravenes Section 99 of Republic Act (RA) No. 8550 or the “Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998” as amended, which prohibits the conversion of mangroves for any other purpose, as well as RA No. 8371 or the “Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Act of 1997”, if mangrove areas are located within ancestral domains. The resolution also cited Presidential Proclamation 2152, which declares the entire Province of Palawan and certain parcels of the public domain and/or parts of the country as mangrove swamp forest reserves. The Global Mangrove Alliance Philippines (GMAP) welcomed De Lima’s measure “as an important opportunity to ensure that decisions affecting our mangroves are guided by science, existing environmental laws, the constitutional right of Filipinos to a balanced and healthful ecology, and the long-term welfare of our communities". “Available evidence also indicates that successful earth-balling has been demonstrated primarily for young, small-diameter mangroves. Most trees affected by development projects are mature mangroves, making successful transplantation highly uncertain and ecologically risky,” GMAP said in a statement. Coastal greenbelt zones sought Relatedly, De Lima also filed House Bill (HB) No. 8353 seeking to require the establishment of coastal greenbelt zones, which are mangroves and beach forests stretching to at least 100 meters in width, designed to prevent coastal erosion. The measure also specifically defines the country’s policy goals and objectives for the management of mangrove resources in the country. “The lack of a national policy on mangroves poses a great challenge and has caused existing mangrove protection and rehabilitation efforts to remain ineffective and unsuccessful," she noted in her bill. De Lima says a "comprehensive mechanism" must be urgently implemented to address this.

Mayor Wes clarifies use of Valenzuela vehicle seen at airport. Valenzuela City Mayor Weslie “Wes” Gatchalian clarified on Sunday, Aug. 30, that a city government vehicle seen at the airport was used to transport Baby Ayla and her mother ahead of the child’s liver transplant in India. The clarification came after a Facebook post questioned why a Valenzuela City vehicle marked “Strictly for Official Use Only” was seen at the airport. Gatchalian said the passengers were Baby Ayla and her mother, who were being assisted by the city government for their trip abroad. “Isang paglilinaw lang po, ang sakay ay si Baby Ayla at nanay niya (Just to clarify, the passengers were Baby Ayla and her mother),” he said. Baby Ayla, a Valenzuela resident diagnosed with biliary atresia, left for India on Sunday for an urgent liver transplant. The city government earlier provided financial assistance for the family’s airfare and hotel accommodation during the child’s operation and recovery in India. The assistance was coordinated through the City Social Welfare and Development Office (CSWDO). The city had also previously extended medical assistance to Baby Ayla’s family in October 2025, while the CSWDO continued monitoring the case in March 2026. Doctors had recommended an urgent liver transplant. Although assistance through a foundation partner at the Chinese General Hospital was initially considered, the family later decided to have the procedure in India. Mag-verify muna bago mag-share (Please do not be part of spreading fake news or misinformation. Verify information first before sharing),” he said. The city government also asked the public to pray for Baby Ayla’s safe journey, successful transplant, and recovery.

Manila police check Mendiola security setup for Heroes’ Day protests. The Manila Police District (MPD) inspected its security preparations at Mendiola, Manila, on Monday, Aug. 31, as various groups hold protests and activities for National Heroes Day. MPD Chief Brig. Gen. Atty. Arnold C. Santiago personally led a simulation exercise and evaluation of the police deployment, barriers, and other security equipment in the area. The activity was conducted pursuant to the directive of NCRPO Chief Brig. Gen.Christopher N. Abrahano to simulate the installation of metal and concrete barriers and container vans at seven strategic gates or entry points around Malacañang. Police also monitored the area for possible developments involving protest groups. Santiago inspected the barriers and strategic security points in Mendiola to assess the positioning of police personnel and equipment and ensure a prompt response to possible incidents. The MPD said its security preparations would be carried out under the principle of maximum tolerance, with police tasked to maintain peace and order while respecting the public’s right to peaceful assembly and expression. Police said the simulation and evaluation were intended to ensure the safety of protesters, police personnel, and other members of the public while preventing situations that could lead to confrontation or disorder. The MPD said it would remain on alert and continue monitoring developments in the area throughout the National Heroes Day activities.

On National Heroes Day, senators urge Filipinos to remember their legacy, build a better nation. Senators on Monday, August 31 called on Filipinos to remember the legacy left behind by the country’s heroes and use this as an inspiration to build a better Philippines. Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian led the Senate in pushing for this call as the country observes this year’s National Heroes Day. “As we honor the men and women whose sacrifices secured our freedom, sovereignty, and democracy, let us remember that their legacy calls on us to continue building a better nation,” Gatchalian said. “Magiging mas makabuluhan ang sakripisyo ng ating mga bayani kung bawat isa sa atin ay maglilingkod sa pamilya, komunidad, at bayan nang may integridad, katapatan, at malasakit (The sacrifice of our heroes will become more meaningful if each of us serves our family, community, and country with integrity, honesty, and compassion),” he further said. Gatchalian also said the recent problems facing the country should spur Filipinos to do their part in protecting public funds and ensure that every program of the government is sincerely for the benefit of the country. “Sa gitna ng mga problemang kinakaharap ng bansa — tulad ng pagbaha, korapsyon sa gobyerno, mga hamon sa kalidad ng edukasyon, at mataas na presyo ng pagkain at kuryente — sama-sama nating pangalagaan ang kaban ng bayan at tiyaking bawat programa ng pamahalaan ay maayos, tapat, at tunay na nagsisilbi sa bawat pamilyang Pilipino (Amidst the problems facing the country—such as flooding, government corruption, challenges regarding the quality of education, and the high cost of food and electricity—let us work together to safeguard public funds and ensure that every government program is well-managed, honest, and genuinely serves every Filipino family),” he said. Real heroes do not ‘ghost’ Sen. Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan, on the other hand, said this year’s celebration of National Heroes Day should serve as a reminder that real heroes do not ghost. “Madalas natatapat ang Araw ng mga Bayani sa ghost month — paalala na ang tunay na bayani, hindi nanggo-ghost (National Heroes' Day often falls during the “Ghost Month”—a reminder that a true hero doesn't “ghost”),” Pangilinan said. The senator further pointed out that the commemoration of National Heroes Day is rooted in acknowledging the collective struggle for freedom that began with the Revolution of 1896. The annual exercise is a means to pay tribute not only to the renowned heroes found in history books but, above all, to the unsung Filipinos who bravely love their country. He pointed out that many of these heroes come to the aid of those on the brink of peril, even at the cost of their own health, safety and livelihood. “Sabi nga nila, not all heroes wear capes. Nandyan lang silang: Mga magulang, marami sa kanila mga overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), na araw-araw nagsasakripisyo upang maitaguyod at mabigyan ng mas magandang kinabukasan ang kanilang pamilya; mga environment defender na nangangalaga sa ating lupa, kagubatan, karagatan, at mga komunidad (As the saying goes, not all heroes wear capes. They are right there among us: Parents—many of whom are OFWs—making daily sacrifices to provide for their families and secure a better future for them; environmental defenders who safeguard our lands, forests, oceans, and communities),” Pangilinan explained. “Mga magsasaka at mangingisda, na nagpapakain sa bayan, kahit ginigipit ng price manipulators at smugglers; at mga truth-tellers, kasama ang mga saksi sa mga krimen, na naninindigan para sa tama at pananagutan kahit binabantaan o sinusuhulan (Farmers and fisherfolk who feed the nation, even while being exploited by price manipulators and smugglers; and truth-tellers—including witnesses to crimes—who stand up for what is right and for accountability, despite facing threats or offers of bribes),” he stressed. Pangilinan further hailed as heroes the country’s riders, social workers, health professionals, disaster and emergency response volunteers who braved the recent floods to serve fellow Filipinos. “Hinarap nila ang panganib para maghatid ng pagkain, gamot, tulong, at kaligtasan. They faced danger to deliver food, medicine, aid, and safety,” he noted. “‘Yan ang bayaning Pilipino: Hindi nagpapasiil sa hamon ng buhay (That is the Filipino hero: one who does not yield to life's challenges),” he reiterated.
